Each of them will cost you something, and each of them will say who you are to be, in London, for the next ten years.

options.label: Let Lestrade Charge Him with the Park Lane Murder and Keep Out of It.
options.detail: The credit goes to the Yard, and the name stays with Lestrade. You are not in it. It is the plain way, and it will hold, if the case has been built.
options.outcome: You say that to him, and only to him, belongs the credit of the arrest. He is a little stiff, and then a little moved. He writes the charge in a firm, round hand, and the pen does not once stop.
options.requiresHint: Needs evidence that would hold in court

options.label: Give the Evidence Yourself in Open Court and Let London Know.
options.detail: A dead man who walks into the Old Bailey is a thing that the papers will not stop talking about. It is a stronger case, and the end of your quiet, and the Professor's friends will know where to find you.
options.outcome: You say that you will appear. Lestrade stares at you for a moment as if you had proposed to walk across the Thames. Then he grins, and offers to hold your hat.
options.requiresHint: Needs evidence that would hold in court

options.label: Sit with the Colonel in the Cell and Make Him Talk.
options.detail: He has been at the top of his trade for thirty years, and he has a great deal to tell. Shown the case against him, in full, from the beginning, a prisoner will sometimes choose his own ending.

quote.speaker: Colonel Moran
quote.text: You have the thumb and the gun, Mr Holmes, and the boy at Park Lane and the window. I see that I should be a fool to deny any of it. What do you wish to hear first?

options.outcome: You sit on a stool at the door of the cell, and lay it out for him, piece by piece, as if for a lecture. He listens without a word. At about four o'clock he asks for a pencil. He has been accurate all his life, and cannot bear to be wrongly described.
options.requiresHint: Needs the window, and the cards, the gun or the sentinel

options.label: Ask Mycroft to Settle It Quietly and Keep the Country's Name Out of It.
options.detail: A colonel of the Indian Army in the dock is a scandal that will reach three Ministers. There are ways of settling it that no jury will see, and your brother has them all in his desk.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: He is to be sent to an island in the Indian Ocean, Sherlock, where he will have a comfortable house and no rifle. It is not justice. It is, however, an arrangement.

options.outcome: Your brother arrives at four in a closed carriage, with a paper that has been signed by someone whom neither of you will name. It is all neat. The Adair family will be told that the case is closed. You keep your eyes off Lestrade while the paper is read.

options.label: Charge Him on What You Have and Hope.
options.detail: It is thin. It is a charge, and a name, and a bullet and an arrest in an empty house. A good counsel will take it to pieces, and a good counsel is what the Colonel can afford.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I'll write it, sir, if you say so. It has lost a good many that it hadn't a reason for.

options.outcome: He writes it, with a face like a pall. It is a charge that will bring the Colonel to the Old Bailey in June, and it will bring him there in a good coat, with a good counsel, and a clear voice.

echoes.text: He was taken alive, and that is what makes every choice below possible.
Watson is sitting on the other side of the fire with a bandage and a cigar. He looks like someone who would like to be asked.
The bullet from the bust is on the table in front of you, flattened against the wall of your own sitting-room.

D1.title: The Stick
D1.description:
Wednesday 9 October 1889, a little before ten in the morning. Dr Watson has gone out and left a stick behind him, or so you thought. It is not his. It is a stout malacca with a silver band, chewed at the handle by something with strong teeth, and it was left on the table by a visitor who has just been shown up the stairs.

The band says that it was presented to James Mortimer, M.R.C.S., by his friends of the C.C.H., and gives the year 1884. The footsteps on the stair are those of a tall, stooping man with a dog at his heel. You have the time of a long breath to say what you make of him.

options.label: Read the Stick and Tell Him What It Says.
options.detail: A stick is a man's autobiography in a small hand. The band, the bite and the ferrule will give you a doctor, a dog and a country practice before he has hung up his hat.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: Remarkable, Mr Holmes. The hospital was Charing Cross, the year was my leaving, and the dog is a curly-haired spaniel. I had been told that you were exact. I had not expected to be undressed in the doorway.

options.outcome: He is delighted, and so is the spaniel. Dr Mortimer is a tall, thin, shambling man of thirty or so, with a long nose and kind eyes, and he has come two hundred miles with something in his breast-pocket that he is afraid of. You get him into the armchair, and he takes out a roll of yellowed paper.

options.label: Ask Him Plainly What Has Brought Him from Dartmoor.
options.detail: He has been on the stair for three minutes with his courage in his hand. Anyone who has been invited to explain himself will not need to be impressed.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: I am a country doctor, Mr Holmes, and I am out of my depth. A friend of mine is dead, and there is another who will come to London tomorrow, and between them they have made me frightened of a thing that I cannot believe in.

options.outcome: He is grateful, and shows it by talking too fast. You let the stick lie. Someone who is afraid for another man will tell the truth in the order in which it hurts, and you have always preferred it so.

options.label: Take the Spaniel's Part and Let Him Warm to You.
options.detail: A dog that has walked two hundred miles at heel is a better reference than any letter. The doctor will be easier once the animal is.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: He does not take to everyone, Mr Holmes. He took to you in the doorway. I am obliged to him. It is a thing that I have never had to explain to a client before.

options.outcome: The spaniel puts its chin on your knee, and the doctor says that this is the first time in a week that he has seen his companion at ease. You scratch its ear. It is a pleasant, ridiculous, unlooked-for beginning to a case that is not going to be pleasant at all.

D2.title: The Legend of Hugo
D2.description: Wednesday 9 October 1889, half-past ten. The manuscript is dated 1742 and is in the hand of a Baskerville to his sons. It says that in the time of the Great Rebellion a wild squire called Hugo carried off a farmer's daughter to Baskerville Hall, and locked her in an upper room, and sat down to drink with his friends. She escaped by the ivy. He followed her across the moor with his hounds, in a rage, and was found at dawn with his throat torn out, and over him a great black beast with eyes of fire. Since then, it says, the family has died hard. Dr Mortimer reads it in a low voice, with his eyes on the fire. When he has finished, nobody speaks.

options.label: Ask Whether He Believes a Word of It.
options.detail: A person who has brought you a ghost story had better say whether he is frightened of the ghost or of what the ghost is for.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: As a man of science, no. As someone who has walked that moor at night, Mr Holmes, I would not care to say. Sir Charles believed it. It was the death of him, I think, whatever the coroner found.

options.outcome: He takes off his glasses and wipes them for a long time. He is a good, plain, honest doctor, and he has been ashamed for two months of what he has been thinking. You put the paper down and tell him that the shame is a waste of his time.

options.label: Ask for the Newspaper Account of Sir Charles's Death.
options.detail: A legend is a story, and a story can be dressed. The inquest is a record, and it can only be read.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: I have the Devon County Chronicle in my coat. The verdict was that he died by the visitation of God. I was the doctor, Mr Holmes, and I signed the paper. I did not say what I had seen on the path.

options.outcome: He gives you the cutting, and you read it twice. It is an honest piece of local reporting, and it says that Sir Charles was found on the Yew Alley, with the gate shut behind him, and that there was no mark of violence. It does not say what is in the doctor's face.

options.label: Ask Who Else Lives Near the Hall.
options.detail: A great house on a moor has a few neighbours, and each of them knows something. It is the neighbours who write the legends.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: There is the naturalist, Mr Stapleton, and his sister, at Merripit House. There is Mr Frankland of Lafter Hall, who goes to law as other men go to church. And there are the Barrymores, who keep the Hall.

options.outcome: He counts them on his long fingers, and you note them as he goes. Four households within ten miles, a great mire, and a prison on the moor. It is a smaller world than a London street, and it is as full of motives.

D3.title: The Footprints
D3.description: Wednesday 9 October 1889, noon. Dr Mortimer has told the rest. Sir Charles Baskerville walked every night after dinner in the Yew Alley at the back of the Hall, and on the last night of his life he stood a long time at the moor-gate, smoking, and then went on up the avenue. The doctor found him at the end of it, on his face. There was nothing on the body, and a great deal on the ground. A little way from the corpse, on the turf, he had seen the footprints of an animal. He tells you the size of them in a voice that he has to steady.

options.label: Ask How Sir Charles Was Walking in the Alley.
options.detail: A man's tread on gravel is a record of his state of mind. If he walked on his toes, he was not walking, and the question is what from.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: On his toes, Mr Holmes, the whole of the way from the gate. I have thought about it every night for two months. A man does not tiptoe along an alley who is walking towards a danger. He does it who is running from one.

options.outcome: This is the best thing that anyone has said in the room. You sit up in your chair, and the doctor sees the light come into your face, and at last he looks less like anyone who is carrying a ghost and more like a person who is carrying a clue.

options.label: Ask Whether the Animal's Marks Were Those of a Dog.
options.detail: The doctor saw them, and he is no fool. If they were a dog's, a dog is the answer, and the legend is a dressing.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: I have seen a great many dogs, Mr Holmes, and I said that it was a hound. But it was twice the size. I would have told the coroner so, if I had thought he would write it down.

options.outcome: He says it in a rush, like a man taking a pill, and sits upright. You do not smile, because it is not a smiling matter, and you do not say that he is mistaken, because you have never yet known a frightened doctor to be mistaken about a footprint.

options.label: Ask Who Gains by Sir Charles's Death.
options.detail: There is a motive in the manuscript, and a hound in it. There is also, in the will, a name, and the name is what a court will want.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: The heir is the nephew, Sir Henry, who is coming from Canada. He has had no idea of the estate until I wrote to him. After him there is nobody nearer than a cousin whom nobody has seen in twenty years.

options.outcome: You take down the name of the cousin, and the name of the late brother, and the year. A man may be very much interested in a fortune and very little in the man who has it. You make no remark, and the doctor, who is not a stupid man, looks at you and then at the floor.

echoes.text: The doctor has told you what he believes, and you have decided that he is right to be afraid.

D4.title: Sir Henry Baskerville
D4.description:
Thursday 10 October 1889, half-past nine in the morning. Sir Henry Baskerville comes up the seventeen steps in a ruddy, weather-beaten, brown suit of a cut that nobody in London would have worn, and puts a sheet of paper on your table. He is thirty, strongly built, with thick black eyebrows and the frank, impatient manner of someone who has spent his life on a ranch.

That is the first letter that he has had in England. It was waiting at the Northumberland Hotel. It is made of words that have been cut from a newspaper and pasted on a half-sheet of paper, and it says, in print, that if he values his life or his reason he will keep away from the moor.

options.label: Hold the Letter to the Light and Name the Newspaper.
options.detail: A sheet that has been pasted from a newspaper is a sheet that was cut from one. The type, the paper and the glue will say which, and where it was done.
options.outcome: Sir Henry is more impressed than he is willing to say. Dr Mortimer, who has been sitting quiet, remarks that the thing is no more like a ghost than a telegram is. It is a good remark. This is the first sensible thing that has been said on the subject for two months.

options.label: Ask Sir Henry What Enemies a Man from Canada Can Have.
options.detail: Someone who has never been in England has made few enemies here. The ones that he has made, he will not have made on purpose.

quote.speaker: Sir Henry Baskerville
quote.text: I have none, sir, that I know of. I came over to take a house, and I find I'm to be warned off it by a man with a pair of scissors. It makes me want to take the house more.

options.outcome: He laughs, and shows a set of excellent teeth. Watson, on the sofa, nods at him as if he had passed an examination. You say that anyone who is not afraid is a great deal harder to protect, and Sir Henry, who has not before been told this, is silent for a moment.

options.label: Send Cartwright to Every Hotel Near Charing Cross for a Torn Times.
options.detail: A person who cuts a leading article leaves the rest of the paper behind him. It is in a waste-paper basket within a mile of the Strand, and a boy can be paid to look.
options.outcome: You write a short list of the hotels on the back of an envelope, and the boy is out on the stair in a minute, with the envelope in his fist. Sir Henry looks after him with a mixture of amusement and respect. In England, he says, it is done with boys.

D5.title: Three Broken Threads
D5.description: Friday 11 October 1889, after breakfast. The hunt for the paper has gone cold, and three other ends are in your hand. A bearded man in a hansom followed Sir Henry and Dr Mortimer from the door of the hotel and down Regent Street, and the cab number is in Watson's notebook. A new brown boot, put outside the door of Sir Henry's room at night to be cleaned, has not come back. And a butler at Baskerville Hall has been written to on a question that only he could answer, and a telegram is waiting at Baker Street. You have until the evening to pull one of them tight.

options.label: Trace the Hansom Through the Cabman.
options.detail: A cab has a number, and a number has a stand, and a cabman will talk to a gentleman who wants to hire him for a day. It is the shortest of the three threads, and the one that is most likely to snap.
options.outcome: You take a cab to Shipley Yard in Southwark with the number in your notebook and a half-sovereign in your waistcoat. It is a long, wet, uncomfortable ride, and you spend it thinking about beards.

options.label: Hunt for the Boot.
options.detail: A boot is a small thing to steal and an odd one. Anyone who wanted a stranger's scent would take a thing that had lain on his foot.
options.outcome: You go back to the Northumberland Hotel, where the manager is waiting at the door with his hands behind him and the face of a man who expects to be sued.

options.label: Put Barrymore to the Test with a Telegram.
options.detail: He is the one man at the Hall who could have written to the hotel and be at the Hall the same night. A telegram to the post-office will say whether he was.
options.outcome: You send a wire to the post-office at Grimpen, in the plainest words that you can find, and sit down to wait for an answer that will take three hours.

D5A.title: Clayton the Cabman
D5A.description: Friday 11 October 1889, the afternoon. The cab was Clayton's, of Shipley Yard, Southwark, and Clayton himself is a thickset man of fifty with a red face and a whip. He is happy to talk about a fare, and when you have put half a sovereign on the stand he is happier. The man, he says, was a well-set gentleman with a black beard, who had stopped him at the corner of Trafalgar Square, and sat in the cab for two days, never getting out. He paid by the hour, and gave his name. Clayton scratches his head. It was an odd name for a fare to give.

options.label: Ask the Name and Let Him Say It.
options.detail: Someone who gives his name to a cabman has given it for a purpose. It is the purpose that is worth having, and it is generally in the name.

quote.speaker: Clayton
quote.text: Mr Sherlock Holmes, sir. He said it plain, and told me to put it in my book. I did, and he laughed, and said I'd made a good bargain. I never saw the like.

options.outcome: You throw back your head and laugh. That is the best thing that anyone has said of you this year. Whoever the bearded man is, he has a sense of humour, and he has been following you as closely as he has been following Sir Henry.

options.label: Hire Clayton for a Week to Find the Bearded Man Again.
options.detail: A cabman who has been paid twice is a cabman who looks about him. It is a poor, slow, honest way, and it is the only way that will not alarm the quarry.

quote.speaker: Clayton
quote.text: A week, sir? At my rate? Why, I'd drive him to Dover for it. If he's in London I'll find him, and if he isn't I'll tell you where he's gone. That's a promise.

options.outcome: He touches his hat, and goes off whistling. A cabman is the most useful of all the street's eyes, and the most easily bought. You have a feeling that you have not seen the last of the bearded man, and that Clayton will.

options.label: Take Down the Bearded Man's Description Exactly.
options.detail: A black beard is a thing that can be bought. A pair of eyes, a gait and a manner of sitting in a cab cannot, and Clayton has sat looking at them for two days.

quote.speaker: Clayton
quote.text: Well set, sir, and about forty. He'd a way of looking over his shoulder, and he sat as if he was keeping himself in. And I'll tell you what. He wasn't a London man. I'd put him down for a person who'd lived in the country.

options.outcome: It is not much, and it is more than the Yard has had in its hands for a month. You write it down in your own shorthand, and tell Clayton that he has done well. A false beard on a forty-year-old countryman is a thing that you will not forget.

D5B.title: The Missing Boot
D5B.description: Friday 11 October 1889, late in the afternoon. By four o'clock a second boot has gone from the Northumberland Hotel. It was an old black one this time, and it was taken from the corridor outside the door of Sir Henry's room. Sir Henry has been to the manager, and the manager has been to the hall porter. The hall porter has been to the boots, who has said that he has never in his life lost two of a gentleman's boots in a day. The hotel is in an uproar. Cartwright has come back with an empty envelope and a red face. He has done nine hotels, and has found nothing but a great many baskets.

options.label: Ask What Was Left Behind.
options.detail: A thief who takes a new brown boot, and then an old black one, does not want a pair. He wants to try something on a dog.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: Two boots in two days, neither of them a pair. One was new and one was old, and the old one was the only one that had been worn. He did not want a boot. He wanted a scent, and he took the thing that had the most of it.

options.outcome: It is as plain as day, and no more welcome. Whoever it is, he wants a hound to follow Sir Henry by the smell of him. You say so to Sir Henry, who goes white, and then, being a Baskerville, red.

options.label: Send Cartwright Round the Rest of the Hotels with the Boot's Description.
options.detail: A boy can be sent where a policeman cannot, and a boot is a thing that anyone will look at twice if he has been told to. It is a long, dull search.

quote.speaker: Cartwright
quote.text: Fourteen more, sir, and I'll look in the bins, and I'll ask the boots. If it's in London, I'll have it by Monday. If it ain't, I'll know where it isn't.

options.outcome: He is off with the envelope and a half-crown, with his cap over one ear. It is a thin hope, and you know that it will come to nothing. But a boy who has a task is a boy who is not in the way, and Cartwright is the sort who is happiest when he is running.

options.label: Say Nothing and Give Sir Henry the Boots Yourself.
options.detail: He will go down to Devonshire in the old boots that he has, and there will be no reason in the world for anyone to think that the thing has been noticed.

quote.speaker: Sir Henry Baskerville
quote.text: I'll tell you what it is, Mr Holmes. I came from a country where a man's boots are his own business, and I mean to keep them so. Whoever has them is welcome to the rest.

options.outcome: He laughs, shakily, and lays down a sovereign for the porter. It is a pleasant, courageous, entirely foolish gesture, and it makes you like him the better. You do not like to think what it will mean on the moor.

D5C.title: The Grimpen Telegram
D5C.description:
Friday 11 October 1889, five in the afternoon. The wire to the post-office at Grimpen says, in the plainest words that you could devise, that you wish to know whether the message to Mr Barrymore of Baskerville Hall has been delivered to him in person. It takes three hours to get an answer.

It is a single, short, official sentence, signed by the postmistress, and it says that the message was given by the postmaster's boy into Mr Barrymore's own hands at the Hall. It is not what you had hoped for. It is not what you had feared. It is something that looks, to a hasty eye, very much like the end of a thread.

options.label: Ask Whether the Boy Saw the Butler's Face.
options.detail: A man's hands may take a telegram while the rest of him is somewhere else. A boy who has delivered a thousand of them will know if the man was at home.
options.outcome: You go over it once more, and cannot make it bend. Barrymore was at the Hall. It is a negative that you accept, and you strike him from the list in the notebook. It is the second time this week that a straight answer has been the most disappointing thing in the room.

options.label: Ask Who Else at the Hall Has Been Away This Week.
options.detail: A butler who is in his hall proves that the butler is in his hall. A groom, a cook or a wife is another matter, and a postmistress knows everyone's business.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: Mrs Barrymore has not been away. Nobody at the Hall has been away. But the postmistress says, without being asked, that Mrs Barrymore has been crying for a week, and that she has been told not to say why.

options.outcome: It is gossip, and it is the best that you have had. A woman who cries for a week in a lonely house has a reason, and the reason is on the moor. You make a note of it in the margin, and underline it twice.

options.label: Leave the Butler Alone and Think About the Wire.
options.detail: A telegram that does what it was meant to do is a telegram that was not worth sending. You have spent a shilling, and it is not the shilling that is the loss.
options.outcome: You say that it is neither, and light a pipe. It is the quiet of someone who has run a long way up a blind alley and is deciding whether to run back. Watson, who knows the signs, says nothing more, and brings you the evening paper.

D6.title: Who Goes Down
D6.description: Friday 11 October 1889, nine at night. Sir Henry is determined to go to the Hall on Saturday, and cannot be moved from it. He will take his seat, he says, and he will take his chance, and he is very much obliged to everyone. Dr Mortimer will go with him. You have a case in the Strand that you cannot leave, you tell them, and you say it so smoothly that Watson, who knows that you have no such thing, looks at the fire. You have been in London three days with a hound in your head. You do not mean to leave London yet. You mean someone to go, and you mean that someone to be your eyes.

options.label: Send Watson Alone and Let Everyone Think You Are in London.
options.detail: A person who is thought to be in the Strand is anyone who need not be on guard against. It is Watson's pen that will tell you everything, and your own two feet that will do what it cannot.
options.outcome: He puts his revolver in the pocket of his travelling coat, as if he were not doing it, and says that he would be glad of the exercise. You press his hand. He is the best man in England for this work, and the least likely to take it as a compliment.

options.label: Send Watson and Give Him Cartwright as a Runner.
options.detail: A boy who can carry a message across a moor is a boy who can carry food to a hut. It is a thread that you will want, if the thing goes as you think it must.

quote.speaker: Cartwright
quote.text: To Devonshire, sir? On a train? I've never been out of London in my life. I'll be sharp, sir. I won't be seen, and I won't be late.

options.outcome: You send him for a ticket, and he goes, with the whole of his body trembling with joy. It is a modest investment of a boy, and you think that it will pay. A great many men have been saved in this world by the arrival of the right small thing at the right time.

options.label: Send Watson and Ask Lestrade to Hold Two Men in Readiness.
options.detail: A pair of plain-clothes men and a warrant, held at Exeter, may be in a village in five hours. It is an expense that the Yard will not like, and a security that you will.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Two men at Exeter, and a warrant I haven't got, for a hound nobody's seen. I'll do it, Mr Holmes. I'll come myself if you need me.

options.outcome: He grumbles, and writes it down. You wire Exeter, in his name, with a cypher that the Yard is slow to forget. Lestrade is the least imaginative man in the force, and you would not for the world have any other at your back.

echoes.text: Sir Henry has kept his old boots, and says that he intends to wear them down the platform.

D7.title: Paddington
D7.description:
Saturday 12 October 1889, a quarter to ten in the morning. Platform 3 at Paddington is full of porters and trunks, and Sir Henry Baskerville is standing in the middle of them with his bag in his hand and his face turned to the train.

Dr Mortimer is at his elbow. Watson has his revolver, a notebook and a pipe. You have an hour in which to tell him what you have not told anyone else, and you may as well tell it now, in the open, among the porters. He will not be able to take a note. He will have to remember, and that is the whole of the art.

options.label: Tell Him Never to Let Sir Henry Out on the Moor Alone.
options.detail: It is the one rule that overrides every other. Anyone who is never alone cannot be run down by a hound, and cannot be walked into a mire.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Never alone, Holmes. I shall sleep across his door if I have to. It will be a strange thing to say to the master of a great house, but I shall say it.

options.outcome: He takes it down in his head as though it were an oath, and perhaps it is. The whistle goes. You stand on the platform with your hat in your hand, and watch the train pull out, and the last you see of Sir Henry is a large brown hand waving from the window.

options.label: Tell Him to Watch the Neighbours and Write Down What They Say.
options.detail: A pen is better than a pistol. A neighbour who is watched will do something, and a neighbour who is written about will have done it on paper.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Stapleton and his sister, and Frankland, and anybody else who offers himself. I shall put down the words and the faces, and you may make the sense of them yourself.

options.outcome: He nods, and writes the three names in the notebook before he has settled in his seat. He is the best of correspondents, you remind yourself, because he does not have an opinion until he has a fact. It is a quality that has been at once your convenience and your despair.

options.label: Tell Him to Say Nothing of You to Anyone, and to Mean It.
options.detail: Someone who thinks that you are in London will not look for you on the moor. The surest way to hide a thing is to let a friend believe in it.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Not a word, Holmes, even to Sir Henry. I dislike it, and I shall do it. It will be like carrying a letter that must not be opened.

options.outcome: He makes a face, and puts his hand on your arm. You are asking a great deal of an honest man, and you know it, and he knows that you know. The train carries him away down the line, and you walk back through the station alone with your plan.

echoes.text: Cartwright is somewhere on the platform, wearing a cap that can be seen across a street, and pretending not to know anybody.
Two men from the Yard are on their way to Exeter in an inside compartment, and are not looking at the train.

D8.title: The First Report
D8.description: Sunday 13 October 1889, the morning post. A fat envelope with a Grimpen postmark lies beside your plate, and the breakfast goes cold. Watson writes as he talks, in a long, honest, unhurried hand, and he has told you everything that he has seen and nothing that he has guessed. You read it twice, and then you put it down and walk to the window. There is a convict on the moor, a butler who has a wife who cries, a naturalist who knew Watson's name, and a long, low cry from the Mire. You can follow one thing from London today. It will have to be the thing that will tell you the most.

options.label: Go to the Yard and Read Selden's File.
options.detail: A convict who has broken out is a convict with a past, and a past is in a file. Lestrade has it, and he will let you see it, if you ask him civilly.
options.outcome: Lestrade is at the Yard before you, with his pipe in his mouth and a file under his arm. He has been expecting you since the post came, and you take the long, cold stair together.

options.label: Find Out Who Mr Stapleton Was Before Dartmoor.
options.detail: A naturalist who has settled on a moor has come from somewhere. It will be a school, a college or a regiment, and an agent will know which.
options.outcome: You take a cab to Chancery Lane with Watson's letter in your pocket and a short list of the names that a schoolmaster might have gone by. It is a bright, cold morning, and the walk is a pleasure.

options.label: Ask the Dog Dealers Who Sold a Large Dog This Autumn.
options.detail: A hound that can pass for a legend must have been bought from somebody. It is a long walk along the Fulham Road, and a dull one, and it is the nearest thing to a witness.
options.outcome: You put on your oldest Devon tweeds and a hat that has seen the rain, and take an omnibus along the Fulham Road. A dog-dealer is a vain fellow, and a country squire is a good audience.

echoes.text: Watson has kept your secret. The letter is signed from the Hall, and not once does it mention London.
Dr Mortimer's stick said a country doctor, Charing Cross and a dog, and he was pleased.
You asked Dr Mortimer plainly what had brought him, and he told you in the order in which it hurt.
Dr Mortimer's spaniel took to you in the doorway.
The coroner found death by the visitation of God, and Dr Mortimer signed it.
Four households lie within ten miles of the Hall: the Stapletons, Frankland, the Barrymores and the prison.
Sir Charles went up the Yew Alley on his toes, as a man runs.
Dr Mortimer saw the prints of a hound twice the size of any that he knew.
Sir Henry is the heir, and after him there is a cousin whom nobody has seen.
The warning to Sir Henry was cut from the Times in a hotel, by somebody in a hurry.
Sir Henry knows of no enemy, and means to go.
Cartwright is hunting twenty-three hotels for the torn Times.
The bearded man gave Clayton the cabman your name.
Clayton the cabman is watching London for the bearded man.
The bearded man is forty, well set, and a countryman.
Two boots in two days, neither of them a pair: somebody wanted a scent.
Cartwright is hunting the hotels again, for the boot.
Barrymore was at the Hall when your telegram came, and answered it.
The postmistress says that Mrs Barrymore has cried for a week.
You let the Grimpen telegram go, and have not been easy about it.
Watson has gone down alone, with a revolver in his travelling coat.
You told Watson never to leave Sir Henry alone on the moor.
Watson is writing down the neighbours and their words.

D9.title: Selden's File
D9.description: Monday 14 October 1889, the forenoon. The file on Selden is thick, grey and dull, and Lestrade has put it in front of you like someone giving away a tooth. Selden was a street-robber of the worst kind. He beat an old woman to death in Notting Hill in 1881 and was taken by a constable in the dark. The Home Office, in an hour of doubt, put off the rope on the plea that he was not in his right mind. He has been in Princetown for eight years. He is, the file says, a coarse, strong, cunning brute, and he has a sister, married to a butler in the West of England.

options.label: Ask Lestrade to Double the Warders on the Moor Road.
options.detail: A person who has been loose for a week will be wanted back. A road that is watched is a road that he will not cross, and he will go where he is not seen.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Princetown'll be glad of the help. They're short of men, and they've been told to shoot if he's seen. I'll tell them to hold their fire if there's a gentleman in the way.

options.outcome: He writes it down with a flat, official face. It is a plain, honest piece of police work, and it will make the moor a great deal less comfortable for Selden. It will also make it more comfortable for Sir Henry. You do not say so.

options.label: Ask Whether He Could Be Given Up Quietly to His Sister.
options.detail: Anyone who has been eight years in a cell and a week on a moor has had enough of both. It would be a thing for the Home Office, and a thing for a careful word.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Give him up quietly? I'd lose my stripes. But I'll not be looking hard on the Barrymore side of the moor, Mr Holmes.

options.outcome: It is as near to a promise as a policeman can give. Lestrade is not a sentimental man, and he does not like to be asked, but there is something in the file that has caught him as it has caught you. A woman whose only living kin is a murderer has a claim on somebody's pity.

options.label: Say That Selden Is Not Your Quarry and Leave the File.
options.detail: A convict is a cry in the night and a face at a window. He is not the man who set a hound at Sir Charles Baskerville, and he must not be allowed to take up your time.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: Selden is a brute with a sister. He is not the cause of anything. He is a thing that happens on the moor, like the weather. I must remember to treat him as a hazard and not as a clue.

options.outcome: You push the file back across the desk, and Lestrade, who has been braced for an argument, looks almost disappointed. You have the one fact that you came for. The rest is a policeman's affair, and you hope that the policeman will be kind.

D10.title: The Schoolmaster
D10.description: Monday 14 October 1889, afternoon. The scholastic agency in Chancery Lane has been a clearing-house for the unsuccessful schoolmasters of England for forty years, and its head clerk is a small, damp, anxious man with a ledger. You have given him a short description of a naturalist, a collector of butterflies and moths, of about forty, and a wife or sister, and you have said that he is now on Dartmoor. The clerk turns the ledger over. A school in the North of England failed in 1884 for lack of boys. A man of that kind had it. He has a name, and a great deal of debt.

options.label: Ask the Name and the Name of the School.
options.detail: Someone who has failed at a school has left a name behind him, and a name can be written to. A school that failed has a creditor, and a creditor has a memory.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: Vandeleur, of St Oliver's, in the North. A schoolmaster, a naturalist and a debtor. A person who fled from his creditors with a wife and a collection of moths. It is exactly the kind of man who would find a moor attractive.

options.outcome: It is a name that means nothing, and a school that means everything. The man who keeps the butterflies on Dartmoor is a person who has had a failed school behind him, and a failed school is a place where a man learns to have two names. You write to the creditors.

options.label: Ask Whether a Baskerville Was Ever Connected with the School.
options.detail: Anyone who is in debt and has a collector's passion may also have a family. It is the family that you would like to know about, and the agent may have heard.

quote.speaker: The head clerk
quote.text: A Baskerville, sir? There was a Mr Vandeleur who spoke of an uncle in Devon, once, when he was in his cups. I put it down to the drink. Gentlemen of that sort have a great many uncles.

options.outcome: He says it with the vague, apologetic air of someone who has never been listened to. This is the first hint, and the only one, that the naturalist may have a claim on the house in which Sir Henry is sleeping. You thank him, and give him a sovereign, and he stares at it as at a ghost.

options.label: Say That It Is Enough to Know the Failure and Leave the Rest.
options.detail: Someone who is poor and has a reason to be on a moor has a motive. You need only to have been told that he has debts, and you can leave the name to the Yard.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: A poor man, a collector and a debtor. It is the common run of men on Dartmoor. I must not be so pleased with a motive that I forget that nine out of ten poor men are not murderers.

options.outcome: You go out into Chancery Lane with a slight smile, and a feeling of having done something clever and slightly wasteful. The Strand is full of men who are poor, and you are nearly the only one who is about to be told why.

D11.title: The Fulham Road
D11.description:
Monday 14 October 1889, the afternoon and evening. The Fulham Road has more dealers in dogs than any street in London, and you have been up and down it for four hours in the character of a Devon squire who wants a guard for a lonely house.

You have been shown a great many mastiffs, a Newfoundland that was sorry for itself, and a bull-terrier with a good opinion of its own jaws. Nobody has sold a really enormous dog this autumn to a gentleman from the West. At the end of the road is a shop with a green blind, and a brass plate that says Ross and Mangles.

options.label: Go In and Ask Mr Mangles for the Biggest Dog That He Has Sold.
options.detail: A dealer is a vain man about his biggest animal. He will tell you who had it, and for what, if you give him the chance to boast.

quote.speaker: Mr Mangles
quote.text: Sold him a cross-breed in September, sir, a mastiff and a bloodhound, the biggest I ever had in the shop. A gentleman from the West Country, who paid cash and wouldn't give his name. He took it away in a crate.

success.outcome: He talks for ten minutes, and you hear the sale from the beginning to the end. A mastiff and a bloodhound, black, sixty inches at the shoulder, bought in September, taken to Paddington in a crate, and the gentleman had a naturalist's net on the seat of his cab. You walk out with the date, the weight and a small, sharp thrill.

failure.outcome: He is a surly man, and he has had a bad day. He looks at you, and at your Devon tweeds, and tells you that he does not sell dogs to gentlemen who are not going to buy. You come out into the Fulham Road with the evening coming down and nothing in your hands but a card with the shop's name on it.

options.label: Ask the Boy Who Sweeps the Yard.
options.detail: A boy knows what is sold, and to whom, long before his master will say. It will cost a shilling and a little patience, and he will say less than the truth and more than he knows.

quote.speaker: The boy at the shop
quote.text: There was a big 'un, sir, last month, as went in a crate. The gent wanted it kept out of the light. He had a beard, and a funny net. Mr Mangles says he never told no one, but I seen it.

options.outcome: He grins, and holds out a hand that has not been washed since the spring. It is not much of a witness, and you could not put him in a box. But he has seen what you wanted, and it is a boy's account, with all a boy's detail. A beard, a net, a crate that was kept in the dark.

options.label: Give It Up and Go Home to Baker Street.
options.detail: A hound that was bought in London was bought in a hundred shops or a thousand. It may have been bought in Bristol or in Hamburg, and there are better ways of spending an evening.
options.outcome: You take a cab to Baker Street with a pipe unlit in your pocket and a sense of the afternoon's absurdity. It has been a long, dull walk, and it has taught you only that a great many people in London keep dogs. You eat a cold supper, and are cheerful.

D12.title: The Second Report
D12.description: Wednesday 16 October 1889, the second post. The letter is dated the fifteenth, and it is twice as long as the first, and in places it is blotted. Watson has been awake for three nights. A light at a window, a butler, a wife, a convict and a figure on a hill have all been got into one envelope. You read it standing, as you read the best of his work, with your whole body leaning on the table. There are three things in it that matter, and you can pursue one. The rest must wait until a second post, and a second post is a day away.

options.label: Find Out Who Stands on the Tor in the Moonlight.
options.detail: A figure that is not the convict and not a countryman is the one thing in the letter that you cannot place. It is the one thing that you would most like to.
options.outcome: You put down Watson's letter, and spread the map of the moor on the table, and look at the tor for a long time. It is a small hill, and a great many things might be seen from it.

options.label: Ask Dr Mortimer About a Woman Called Lyons.
options.detail: A letter was found in Sir Charles's pocket, and it had on it the initials L.L. The doctor has been a neighbour of the family for years, and the name will be in his notebook.
options.outcome: You write to Dr Mortimer by the evening post, in a hand as plain as you can make it, and ask him for everything that he knows of a woman whose initials are L.L.

echoes.text: Lestrade has said that he will not look hard on the Barrymore side of the moor. You are glad, and you do not say so.
The warders at Princetown have had their orders. The moor road has an extra man at the cross.

D13.title: The Barrymores' Plea
D13.description: Friday 18 October 1889, ten at night. The trunk is half packed, and a wire comes up the stairs. It is a small, painful, humane problem, and it has been set before you by Watson, in three lines. Barrymore wishes to send a convict, who is his wife's only brother, out of England by a ship from Plymouth, and he has asked Sir Henry to give him a suit of clothes. It is, he says, to be an old one, of the sort that Sir Henry has no more use for. The warders will be looking for a man in grey. They will not be looking for a gentleman in tweed. It is an act of pure compassion, and a great risk.

options.label: Let Sir Henry Give the Old Suit.
options.detail: A person who has been eight years in a cell will not be recognised in a good coat, and a sister who has sat up for a week will be kinder for the thing being done. The clothes will smell of Sir Henry.

quote.speaker: Sir Henry Baskerville
quote.text: He is to have my old tweed, and a pair of boots, and welcome. I should be ashamed to be a Baskerville and not do it. If it comes out, I'll say that I did it in my own name.

options.outcome: You wire your assent with a heavy heart. It is a good deed, and it has a thread in it that you do not like. The old coat will go out of the Hall on the shoulders of a man whom everybody on Dartmoor will be looking for, and it will smell, to anything that has a nose, of Sir Henry.

options.label: Have Selden Held in the Hall Until a Ship Is Ready.
options.detail: A convict who is kept in a cellar is a convict who is safe, and a convict who is safe is not a convict who wears a gentleman's coat. It is a harder thing for the Barrymores, and a better one for everyone else.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Hold him, Holmes? In the Hall? With the warders on the road and the whole county looking? It may be done. It will need plenty of nerve, and a little luck, and Barrymore's silence.

options.outcome: It is the dangerous course, and the careful one. Watson will have the convict locked in the wine-cellar, and Barrymore will have the key, and nobody will be allowed upstairs. It is a plain breach of the law, and you think the law will forgive it. You think that Lestrade will.

options.label: Tell Watson to Look the Other Way and Say Nothing.
options.detail: Anyone who sees nothing is anyone who cannot be asked. It is a poor kind of mercy, and it leaves the matter where it was: in the hands of the Barrymores and the weather.
options.outcome: You send the wire, and sit with it for a long time before you light the lamp. It is not a decision. It is the postponement of one, and you are aware that it is the kind that is generally taken for you in the end by a stronger hand than your own.

D14.title: The Man on the Tor
D14.description:
Wednesday 16 October 1889, evening. A figure, standing against the moon on a tor above the Hall, has been seen by two honest men. It was tall, and thin, and still, and it was watching the moor as a sentry watches a gate.

It is not the convict. It is not any labourer on the estate. It is a stranger, and it is somebody who has taken the trouble to be where he can see, without being seen, the whole of the Hall's front. Someone who does that is a person who has either a plan or a purpose. You must decide how to find out which.

options.label: Send Cartwright Up to the Moor with a Rucksack and a Blanket.
options.detail: A boy can sleep in a hole, and carry bread, and say that he is looking for a lost dog. He will come back with a great deal more than he went with.

quote.speaker: Cartwright
quote.text: Up on the tor, sir, in a blanket, with a bit of cheese. I'll be a lost sheep, I will. If there's a gent about, I'll know him by his boots. Nobody ever looks at a boy's.

options.outcome: You wire the instruction to Watson, and ask him to let the boy sleep in the stables. It is a thin plan, and it is the best that you have. A boy who has been trusted with a task will do it better than someone who has been told to be careful.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs Cartwright to be on his way to the Hall

options.label: Tell Watson to Leave the Man Alone and Watch Him from the Hall.
options.detail: A person who is chased is anyone who runs, and a person who runs is someone who knows. It is better to know him, and to be let alone, and to let him think that he is not seen.
options.outcome: It is a quiet, patient, unsatisfactory sort of reply, and you are not surprised that Watson does not like it. But the man on the tor will be there tomorrow night, and the night after, and the longer that he stays, the plainer he will be.

options.label: Make Up Your Mind to Go Down to Devonshire Yourself.
options.detail: Anyone who is on the moor is anyone who can be found there. You will go quietly, by a different station, and take a room in a village that is not Grimpen.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: I have been in London long enough. A report is a thing that a friend writes, and a hound is a thing that a man must meet. I shall go down, and I shall tell nobody, and I shall be where I am least expected.

options.outcome: That is the first time in the case that you have said it aloud, to yourself, in an empty room. A strange, steady feeling comes over you, the feeling of a hunter who has stopped reading the tracks and has decided to follow them. You begin to pack, and you tell nobody.

D15.title: Mortimer on Laura Lyons
D15.description: Wednesday 16 October 1889, late. Dr Mortimer's reply is short, and accurate, and a little shocked. Laura Lyons is the daughter of old Mr Frankland of Lafter Hall, and she married an artist called Lyons who deserted her. Her father has refused to see her since, and she lives in a small house at Coombe Tracey, where she earns a poor living with a typewriter. She is, says the doctor, a pretty, quick, unhappy woman, and Sir Charles gave her charity. He does not say what else. He adds, almost as an afterthought, that Sir Charles had a letter from her in his pocket on the night of his death.

options.label: Ask Whether Anyone Has Spoken to Her About the Letter.
options.detail: A woman who wrote a note to a dead man has been asked a question, or has not. If she has not, it is because someone has been careful.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: I have not spoken to her, Mr Holmes. I thought it best not to. She has had a hard life, and I did not wish to be the man who asked her where she was on the night of the fourth. I see that it was a weakness.

options.outcome: It is the honourable, unprofitable answer of a good man, and you cannot be cross. You ask him to say nothing now, and to put the letter, with its initials, where it can be found. A woman who has been left alone for two months will have had time to prepare.

options.label: Ask Whether She Has Any Claim on the Baskerville Money.
options.detail: A woman who has been a charity case may have been a letter-writer for gain. It is a hard thing to ask, and it must be asked.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: She had none, to my knowledge. Sir Charles gave her small sums, and was to give her more. It was understood that he was going to help her with a divorce. It was a kindness that cost him dear.

options.outcome: A divorce, and a promise. A woman who is waiting for a man's money to free her will be unlikely to wish him dead. It is a point in her favour, and a point against someone else, and you put the two side by side on the page and look at the gap between them.

options.label: Write to Her Yourself and Ask for a Meeting.
options.detail: A letter from a stranger who is polite and persistent is a letter that may be answered. She has a reason to be afraid, and you have a reason to ask. It will go in the morning post.
options.outcome: You sign it with a name that is not your own, and post it yourself. It is a plain, civil, desperate little note, and you are fairly sure that it will frighten her. It may also, which is the point of it, persuade her to say something.

D16.title: The Third Report
D16.description: Friday 18 October 1889, a little after noon. The third envelope is not a letter but a part of a diary, torn out in a hurry and sent by the second post. Watson has seen Laura Lyons. He has seen Frankland and his telescope. He has seen, on the night of the sixteenth, a hand against the moon, and a candle on the tor, and a boy with a bundle. He has not seen the man, and it has been on his mind all day. You put the pages in order, and lay them on the table beside the map. There are three loose ends in them, and one afternoon in which to pull one.

options.label: Write to Frankland and Ask What His Telescope Has Seen.
options.detail: Someone who watches the moor all day with a glass has seen more than the constable. He will not like to be asked, and he will be delighted to tell.
options.outcome: You write to Mr Frankland in your politest hand, and enclose a stamped envelope, and wonder, as you seal it, whether he will take the stamp for an insult.

options.label: Ask Lestrade What Evidence Would Hold a Warrant.
options.detail: A person who has done what you think this man has done will have to be arrested, one day, by someone who has been told what for.
options.outcome: You take a cab to Scotland Yard, and find Lestrade at his desk with his coat off. He has been expecting you. Anyone with a hound to report to the Yard has generally been expected for a week.

options.label: Look into the Baskervilles' Dead Brother.
options.detail: There was a younger brother, Rodger, who went to Central America and is said to have died there. Anyone who is said to be dead has a way of having left a son.
options.outcome: You send for the Baskerville family papers, a pen and a clean sheet, and begin, in a small hand, a pedigree. It has three brothers in it, and one of them has a question-mark.

echoes.text: You have written to Laura Lyons, and not had a reply. Watson's diary says that she was frightened of a visitor, and that the visitor was not you.
Cartwright is on the tor with a blanket. The diary mentions a boy with a bundle. It is odd to read about your own boy, in a stranger's hand.

D17.title: Frankland's Telescope
D17.description:
Friday 18 October 1889, the afternoon. Mr Frankland of Lafter Hall is an old, red, quarrelsome gentleman who has been to law about a right of way, a spring and a rabbit warren, and has lost nearly every time. He has a telescope on the roof of his house, and has used it, with great industry, to observe the movements of his neighbours.

His reply is eleven pages long. It says that a convict is hiding on the moor, which he discovered himself, and that a boy goes every day to the tor with a basket. It says, in the fourth paragraph, that he has seen a gentleman at Merripit House who has no business there.

options.label: Ask Which Gentleman at Merripit and When.
options.detail: Someone who is seen at Merripit House is seen by the one who owns it, and a person who is a gentleman is not a servant. Frankland may have said more than he knows.

quote.speaker: Mr Frankland
quote.text: A tall gentleman, sir, in a dark coat, who goes in at the back at ten at night and comes out before dawn. He is not the Stapletons' friend. Nobody calls at Merripit at that hour, and I have noted it down.

options.outcome: It is eleven pages, and the one fact is in the fourth. Somebody has been visiting Merripit House by night, and the old man has seen it through a glass. You thank him in three, and ask whether he would be good enough to go on watching.

options.label: Ask About the Boy with the Basket.
options.detail: A boy who carries food to a tor is carrying it to someone. If the boy is your own, the old man has seen him. If he is not, you have a rival.

quote.speaker: Mr Frankland
quote.text: A thin boy, sir, with a cap and a bundle, every day at noon. He goes up by the tor road. I have told the constable. It is another example of the way in which this county is governed.

options.outcome: You take it down, with a patient face. If the boy is Cartwright, you will have to tell him to take another path. If he is not, you have a boy who carries food to a man on the tor, and a man on a tor who has a reason to be fed.

options.label: Thank Him and Say Nothing of Your Own Plans.
options.detail: A gentleman who writes eleven pages to a stranger will write twelve to the neighbours. It is wise not to feed his enthusiasm, and wiser to leave him wondering.
options.outcome: You reply in a brisk half-page, with a stamp that has the Queen's head upside down. It is a small, private joke, and it brings you the comfort that small jokes bring. The old man will never forgive you, and you do not mean to be forgiven.

D18.title: What a Warrant Needs
D18.description: Friday 18 October 1889, the afternoon. The room at the Yard is warm and smells of sealing-wax, and Lestrade has taken off his coat. He has listened to a long account of a legend, a pair of boots, a hound that nobody has seen and a man on a hill, and has said nothing. At the end he takes a pencil and writes four words on the blotter: Who, what, when, where. A warrant is a thing that has to be sworn to by someone who has seen something, and so far nobody on the moor has seen anything that a magistrate would call a crime.

options.label: Ask What a Magistrate Would Take from Laura Lyons.
options.detail: A woman who has been the last to speak to a dead man is a witness, and a witness who has something to lose can be persuaded. Lestrade knows how it is done.
options.outcome: He puts the pencil down, and the blotter is a plain white page again. It is the clearest instruction that you have had in a week, and you know that it will be difficult to carry out. The woman will not want to say who asked her to write.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs what Mortimer said about Laura Lyons

options.label: Ask for Men to Be Posted at Coombe Tracey and Grimpen Station.
options.detail: A person who wants to leave the moor will go by one of two roads. It is a heavy way of using the Yard's men, and a sure one, if it is done without noise.
options.outcome: It is a plain, mechanical precaution, and it will do nothing at all unless the man runs. But it is the kind of thing that wins cases, and you are pleased. He puts down the names in a notebook as if he had thought of it himself.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs the men you asked Lestrade to hold at Exeter

options.label: Say That You Will Not Ask for a Warrant Until You Have the Hound.
options.detail: A warrant for a man is a warrant for a name. A warrant for a hound is a warrant for the thing itself, and you would like to have both.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Wait for the hound, is it? I've waited for stranger things. I'll not say I like it, but give me a day's notice and a decent train, and I'll be there.

options.outcome: He grunts and pulls on his coat. It is the reply of a policeman who has been given a theory to carry in one pocket and a doubt in the other. You are fond of him for it. There is a kind of honesty that does not argue, and it is the best kind to take down to Devonshire.

D19.title: Rodger Baskerville
D19.description: Friday 18 October 1889, five in the afternoon. The Baskervilles had three brothers. Sir Charles, who is dead, and Henry, the young man's father, who is also dead, and Rodger, the youngest, who was a black sheep and fled to Central America in 1876, and who is said to have died of yellow fever, unmarried. It is Dr Mortimer's belief, and the Baskerville tradition. You have no reason to doubt it, except that you have never in your life met an heir who was as convenient as that. Anyone who has died abroad is anyone who cannot be asked.

options.label: Ask Mycroft for the Consular Records from Central America.
options.detail: A consul keeps a register of every Englishman who dies in his district, and the register of Costa Rica will say whether Rodger Baskerville is in it. Mycroft has the key to the room where such things are kept.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: There was a Rodger Baskerville, Sherlock, who left a widow and a child at San José in 1876. I find no certificate of his death. I find a note that the widow was last seen on a ship bound for England.

options.outcome: It is a spare, dry piece of information, and it is exactly what you wanted. A widow, a child and a ship. Someone who has been dead for thirteen years may, in the dark, have had a son. You do not say so, even to yourself, until you have written the name on the back of an envelope and looked at it.

options.label: Ask Dr Mortimer to Search the Hall's Family Papers.
options.detail: A great house keeps a great many letters. If there was a widow and a child, there may have been a request to the head of the family, and a refusal.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: I will look, Mr Holmes, but I confess that I have not liked to turn out the library. There are a great many letters in it, and Sir Charles destroyed the worst of them before he died. I shall do what I can.

options.outcome: He will take a week, and be honest about it. It is the slow, scrupulous, unremarkable way. You would have preferred Mycroft's, but you have been waiting for the doctor's help since Wednesday, and you would not wish him to think that you had overlooked it.

options.label: Leave the Dead Brother and Work from What Is in the Letters.
options.detail: A theory that is not yet wanted may be left in a drawer. It will keep, and a person who has too many theories is someone who has stopped looking.
options.outcome: You turn to the third envelope and spread the pages again, as a man puts away a card that he has no immediate use for. The brother will come back. The truth is that you are slightly afraid of him, and that fear, in your own case, is nearly always an indication.

D20.title: The Decision
D20.description:
Friday 18 October 1889, nine at night. The letters have been read, and the inquiries have been made, and the case has reached the point at which nothing more can be done by post. A boy has been fed, a convict has been spoken for, a woman has been written to, and in the dark at the other end of the line a man whom you have never seen is watching a house.

You have a map of the moor on the table, and a ticket in your waistcoat. It is a pleasure to have come to a choice, and an alarm. You have to decide how Sherlock Holmes is to arrive on Dartmoor.

options.label: Go Down by Night, Alone, and Tell Nobody on the Moor.
options.detail: A person who arrives in the dark by a different station is anyone who can be anyone. You will take a room at a farm, or a cave, and be a rumour before you are a face.
options.outcome: You take the night train from Paddington in a shabby ulster, with a bag, a stick and a sketching-block, and sit in a corner of a third-class compartment with a hat over your eyes. A great, cold, uncomfortable calm comes over you, and you sleep as far as Exeter.

options.label: Go Down Openly and Put up at the Hall.
options.detail: Anyone who is expected is a person who is not suspected, and someone who is at the Hall is anyone who can be near Sir Henry. It will tell the neighbours that you are interested.

quote.speaker: Sir Henry Baskerville
quote.text: Come, Mr Holmes! I'd have been glad to have you on the first day. The place wants a bit of London in it. Bring your pipe, and your boots, and I'll have a room aired.

options.outcome: You send a wire in the morning, and Sir Henry replies in an hour, with a cheerful abruptness that you find a relief after a week of Watson's anxiety. The whole of Dartmoor will know within a day that the great detective has come, and the one person whom you wish to know it will be the first.

options.label: Go Down with Lestrade's Two Men and Stay at Princetown.
options.detail: A prison town has a doctor, a chaplain, a governor, and a great many men who are trained to watch a moor. It is a safe, official, uncomfortable base, and a bad one for anyone who wants to go unnoticed.
options.outcome: It is a slow, solid, sensible plan, and it is the one that the Yard would approve. It has the great merit that nobody can be blamed for it. You note, with a faint melancholy, that this is its only merit.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs the men you asked Lestrade to hold at Exeter

echoes.text: You had made up your mind to go down two days ago. The decision is merely a question of how.
A tall gentleman goes in at the back of Merripit House by night, and comes out before dawn. It is on your mind more than anything else on the table.

D21.title: Dartmoor
D21.description: Saturday 19 October 1889, a grey, cold morning. The train leaves you at a wayside halt with a sketching-block, a rucksack and a bad temper, and a great brown country rolls away from the platform on every side. There is not a tree, and hardly a wall. A line of tors stands against the sky like the vertebrae of a beast, and beyond them a green stain lies in the heather that you know, from the map, to be the Great Grimpen Mire. A thin boy in a cap is sitting on a milestone with a bundle on his knee, and is looking at you as a dog looks at a person who may have a biscuit.

options.label: Go Straight to the Stone Hut After Dark.
options.detail: A hut that Watson has found is a hut that a man has left, and a hut that has been left is the best place on the moor to be seen from nowhere. It has a roof, a hearth and a view.

quote.speaker: Cartwright
quote.text: It's a good 'un, sir, up behind the tor. There's a hole for the smoke and a bit of a door. I've been sleeping in the next one, but it's got a hole in the roof.

options.outcome: He grins, and leads you by a sheep-track that has been used by nobody else. It is four miles, and you walk the whole of them with the boy ahead and the tors on either side. You feel as you used to feel on the way to a case in the Alps: small, very well, and as if you were being watched by something enormous.

options.label: Call on Dr Mortimer and Ask for a Map of the Mire.
options.detail: A country doctor knows every path that a patient can take, and the doctor of Grimpen knows the one that a patient cannot. He is a friend, and a silent one.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: Mr Holmes! You are on the moor? I am glad, and I am more frightened than I have ever been. I have the Ordnance sheet, and a note of every spring and bog. The Mire has a path through it, and nobody that I know has found it.

options.outcome: You say that somebody has, and he stares at you in alarm. He spreads out the sheet on his dispensary table, and you spend an hour with a lens and a pencil. By the end of it you have a rough chart of the safe places, and a good idea of where a man would put a marker if he wished to cross.

options.label: Walk the Moor with the Sketch-Block, as an Artist.
options.detail: A painter has a reason to stand still, to look at a hill and to put down a mark. Nobody has ever suspected a painter of anything but bad taste.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: A green stain with a white wand at the edge of it, and another a few yards on, and a third that is nearly out of sight. Someone who plants wands in a mire has a path through it. A person who has a path may use it to be where he should not.

options.outcome: You walk until the light goes, with the block under one arm, sketching tors and tinkers and the side of a cow. By dusk you have a sheet of ugly, honest drawings and a clear idea that someone has laid a line of wands across the Mire. That is the first piece of real knowledge that you have won with your own eyes.

echoes.text: You wrote to Sir Henry, and he has not replied by wire. It is the open road you chose, and you can feel the whole moor watching it.
Cartwright has been waiting here for two days, by his own account, and is in tolerable health.
You left Selden to the Yard, and have not stopped thinking about his sister.
Vandeleur spoke once of an uncle in Devon.
Stapleton is a poor man with debts, and a motive that fits nine men in ten.
A boy at Ross and Mangles saw a bearded gentleman with a net take a crate.
You gave up the Fulham Road, and may have given it up too soon.
You told Watson to leave the man on the tor and watch him from the Hall.
Sir Charles meant to help Laura Lyons to a divorce.
Frankland says that a boy carries a basket to the tor every day at noon.
You kept Frankland at arm's length, and are glad of the quiet.
Lestrade wants Laura Lyons's sworn word before he will ask for a warrant.
You told Lestrade that you would have the hound before you asked for a warrant.
Dr Mortimer is turning out the library for a widow's letters.
You left Rodger Baskerville alone, and he has been at your elbow since.
You came down in the dark, and nobody on the moor knows it but a boy.

D22.title: The Stone Hut
D22.description: Saturday 19 October 1889, evening. The hut is a round of grey stones with a roof of turf and a doorway so low that you go in on your hands. It was built by the first men who lived on this moor, and it has been lived in since, by a series of persons who have been less pleased with it than you are. There is a stove made of a biscuit-tin, a blanket, a pipe, a tin of meat and a lantern, and in the corner a bed of heather. You are cooking your supper when a shadow falls across the doorway. A man is standing against the dusk with a revolver in his hand. It is Watson.

options.label: Tell Him the Whole Plan, from the Beginning.
options.detail: He has been lied to for a week, by you, for his own good. It is the least that you can do to tell him all of it, and to let him be angry first.
options.outcome: He lowers the revolver slowly, and a look comes over his face that is the best compliment that you have ever had. It is relief, and anger, and a great affection, all in the same breath. You sit him down on the heather and give him a mug of tea, and tell him the whole of it, from the stick to the tor.

options.label: Tell Him Only What He Must Know and Send Him Back to the Hall.
options.detail: Anyone who knows less can say less, and a Watson who has not been told a secret cannot give it away, however well he holds his face.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are on the moor, and I am to say nothing and sit across Sir Henry's door as if you were in London. Very well, Holmes. But I shall want to be told why before long.

options.outcome: He takes it very well, and not well at all. He looks at the hut and the stove and the biscuit-tin, and at the face of someone who has not slept in a bed for three nights. You promise him the rest, and he goes off down the hill, with the revolver in his pocket and his head down.

options.label: Tell Him to Say Nothing, Even to Sir Henry, and Mean It.
options.detail: A secret that is shared with one man is a secret. A secret that is shared with two is a conversation. Sir Henry is a good fellow, and cannot hold his tongue.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Not even to Sir Henry, Holmes? I do not like to keep a thing from him, or from anyone. I shall do it, and I shall be most uncomfortable at breakfast.

options.outcome: He makes a wry face, and shakes your hand. It is the second time in a week that you have asked a good man to carry a lie for you, and the second time that he has done it with the air of a soldier taking a hill. You let him go, and you watch him out of sight before you light the stove.

echoes.text: Cartwright has been bringing you bread and tinned meat for a day and a night, and has not once been seen. This is the first piece of luck that you have had on the moor.

D23.title: The Cry on the Moor
D23.description:
Saturday 19 October 1889, the middle of the night. The stove has burned down, and the hut is full of a deep, round silence, the kind that comes before a shout. It comes, from the dark beyond the tor, a long, low, quavering cry, rising and falling, and then a single scream, high and short, that stops as if a hand had been laid across it.

You and Watson are out of the hut and on the heather before you have spoken. There is no moon. There is a light low down in the mist, far away, and something big and swift that moves across it.

options.label: Run to the Cry as Fast as You Can Go.
options.detail: A scream is a summons, and anyone who hears it and does not run is a person who has no right to the name of friend. It is half a mile of heather, in the dark.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: It is a man, Holmes, and he is hurt. I know the sound. Go to the left of the tor, and I shall go to the right, and we shall meet at the bottom.

options.outcome: You go down the hill as a man runs who has been told that his house is on fire. Heather, rock and a runnel of water that is deeper than it looks. Watson runs beside you, with his hand on his pocket. The cry is not repeated. In the darkness ahead there is something white, on the ground, that does not move.

options.label: Go Back to the Hall and Count the Keys of the Cellar.
options.detail: If a convict is locked in a wine-cellar, and the key is on a nail, the cry on the moor is not his. It is a better use of a night than running after a ghost.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: The key is on the nail, Holmes, and the man is asleep in the straw. Whatever that was, it was not Selden. I have never in my life been so glad to see a convict.

options.outcome: You go up the hill at a trot, and in at the kitchen door, and down the stone stair to the cellar, and a lantern shows a coarse, snoring giant in a heap of straw. Barrymore, who has not been to bed, looks at you with terror and thankfulness. The moor has taken somebody else, and it will be a long night.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs Selden held in the cellar at the Hall

options.label: Hold Back and Watch from the Tor.
options.detail: Someone who runs to a trap may run into it. The light that moves on the moor is the thing that has made the cry, and you would like to see it before it sees you.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: A light in the mist, moving at a trot. Not a man's pace. Not a horse's. It went round the base of the tor, and was lost at the edge of the Mire. The cry stopped when it did. I am afraid that I did not like to run.

options.outcome: You lie on the rock, with Watson at your elbow, and watch the shape of the thing that you will have to kill. It is too far, and too dark, for any detail. But the light is steady, and the creature carries it, and it moves as a thing moves that has been taught.

echoes.text: Watson has the whole plan, and the tea has gone cold in his hand.
Watson has half of it, and has said that he will want the rest.
Watson has sworn to say nothing, even to Sir Henry, and has made a face about it.

D24.title: Death on the Moor
D24.description: Sunday 20 October 1889, a little before dawn. The body lies on its face at the foot of a crag, with the neck at an angle that no living man could keep. It is a big, rough, bearded man, in a tweed suit that is a great deal too small for him, and a pair of boots that are very much too new. It is Selden. The coat is Sir Henry's. For a long moment you stand with your lantern raised and your whole mind on the lapel, and you say, to yourself, in a voice that you do not recognise, that this is what the hound was sent to find.

options.label: Watch from the Rocks for Whoever Comes to Look.
options.detail: A person who sets a hound at another man comes to see the result. He will walk up the path with a lantern, and he will be disappointed, and his face will tell you who he is.
options.outcome: You lie behind the rocks with Watson and watch Stapleton examine the dead man. He is a thin, sandy man, with pale, wide eyes, and a deliberate, almost scholarly gentleness in the handling of the corpse. He looks at the coat, and he looks at the boots, and then he looks up at the sky, as one looks at anyone who has cheated.

options.label: Step Out and Meet Stapleton as a Stranger on the Moor.
options.detail: Anyone who is surprised is a person who may say a foolish thing. It is a risk, and it will tell the whole of Dartmoor that Sherlock Holmes is here. It will also, perhaps, tell you who he is.

quote.speaker: Mr Stapleton
quote.text: Mr Holmes! I had heard that you were in London. We are all so honoured. This is a dreadful thing, and the poor creature has been dead for hours. I fear that the coat has led you into an error. I should have said that it was Sir Henry.

options.outcome: He holds out a hand, with a quick, bright smile, and you take it. It is as dry as paper. He is the most agreeable man you have met on the moor, and the best liar. You say that you were thinking of the same error, and he laughs. You have the clear and certain sense that you have told him more than you have learned.

options.label: Read the Dead Man's Boots and the Coat.
options.detail: Someone who has been killed by a hound has a story on his body, and the coat has a maker's label. It is a task for the dark, and it must be done before the light.
options.outcome: It is not pleasant work. You find in the pocket of the tweed coat a pair of spectacles, a blue handkerchief and a letter from his sister. On the inside of the collar is a tailor's label that says, in a neat copperplate, Sir Henry Baskerville, Bart. It is the clearest piece of evidence that you have had since the stick.

echoes.text: You told Watson to look the other way. The old suit left the Hall on the shoulders of a man whom nobody was meant to see.
You approved the gift of the old suit yourself, by wire. It is not a thing that you will say aloud.
You saw the light on the moor, and did not run. It is the choice that you will have to explain to yourself for a good many years.

D24B.title: A Pony in the Mire
D24B.description:
Sunday 20 October 1889, grey dawn. Selden is alive in the cellar, and the Barrymores are crying with relief. The cry that you heard on the moor was not a man's, and you find out whose it was at six in the morning, when a shepherd comes running down to the Hall with news.

There is a dead pony in the edge of the Mire. Its throat has been torn out, and its flank is slashed, and the turf all round it is trodden by something large. A shepherd who has seen the marks says that they are the feet of a dog, and he has been on the moor all his life.

options.label: Go Up and Look at the Pony Yourself.
options.detail: A dead beast is a witness that cannot lie. It will say how big the hound is, and how strong, and how long it was run before it killed.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: The throat is torn clean through, Mr Holmes. I have never seen a dog do that to a pony. I should say it was done by a creature that stood up on its hind legs. The turf is wet, and the prints are plain.

options.outcome: You kneel in the cold heather beside the carcass, with a lens and the doctor's measuring-tape. It is a mess. It is also a clear piece of testimony. The hound is a mastiff-bloodhound cross, taller at the shoulder than a Great Dane, and somebody has trained it to leap.

options.label: Sniff the Dead Pony's Hide for Phosphorus.
options.detail: A beast that has a light on it has been painted. A creature that has been painted has a master, and a master has a pot of paint and a smell.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: Phosphorus? In a pony's hair? Good heavens, Mr Holmes, it is unmistakable. I thought the smell was the Mire. It is on the muzzle, and the throat, and it is fresh.

options.outcome: He bends, and sniffs, and straightens with a face that is partly a doctor's and partly a boy's. The thing is plain. It is neither ghost nor devil. It is a dog, with a coat of luminous paint, and somebody who knows his chemistry. That is the best thing that you have learned all week, and the only one that has made you smile.

options.label: Tell the Shepherd to Say Nothing of It.
options.detail: A moor that is frightened is a moor that talks, and a murderer who hears talk has time to put his tracks in order. A shepherd who is asked to keep quiet may keep quiet.

quote.speaker: The shepherd
