quote.text: I'll not say a word, sir. But there's been a great deal said already. The whole of Grimpen has heard the cry, and they say that old Hugo's out. There's not a man in the village will go out after dark.

options.outcome: He touches his hat. It is the common answer of the country, and it means nothing at all. You know that the cry has gone round the village by noon, and that Stapleton, wherever he is, has heard that a pony has been killed. It is a small, grey, hopeless sort of success.

D25.title: Fixing the Nets
D25.description: Sunday 20 October 1889, the afternoon. The hut is warm, and you have been in it for an hour with a pencil and a map, and the whole thing has come together in your hands. A man with a hound, a house on the edge of the Mire, a wife who is not his sister, a past under another name, and an heir who is not yet dead. It is a good case, and not a bit of it can be proved. You have until the end of the week, and three ways of proceeding. The first is to be bold, the second to be careful, and the third, as usual, to be a little of both.

options.label: Use Sir Henry as the Bait and Take Stapleton in the Act.
options.detail: A person who sets a hound at a baronet will do it again, if he is given the chance. It is a hard thing to say to a brave man, and an easy thing to arrange.

quote.speaker: Sir Henry Baskerville
quote.text: Dine at Merripit on Friday, and walk home alone across the moor? I'll do it, Mr Holmes. I'll do it if you tell me that you will be there. I would sooner be shot at by a man than frightened by a rumour.

options.outcome: He agrees at once, and goes pale, and says that he is much obliged for the compliment. It is a brave, honest, unnecessary promise, and you do not like yourself for asking. But you have asked, and the plan is made, and it is the best that you have.

options.label: Go to Coombe Tracey and Get Laura Lyons to Swear.
options.detail: A statement that has been sworn before a magistrate is a thing that Lestrade can take to a judge. It will take the thing out of the dark, and put it on a table.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: If she'll swear that she wrote the note at his dictation, Mr Holmes, I can have him by Tuesday. Without it, I've got a story about a hound, and a hound can't be arrested.

options.outcome: You write the note by lamplight, and give it to Cartwright. It is the safer course, and the dull one, and it has the whole weight of English law behind it. You cannot see that anything is wrong with it, except that you are not sure that you wish it to succeed.

options.label: Put Watson and Cartwright on Merripit's Garden Wall.
options.detail: A house that is watched from two sides is a house that cannot keep a secret. It will be dull, and cold, and it will tell you where the hound lives.

quote.speaker: Cartwright
quote.text: On the wall, sir? In the dark? With a lantern? I'd sooner be on the wall than on the moor. I've heard the dog, and it ain't a sound I want to meet on a path.

options.outcome: He is brave, and small. You send him with a blanket and a flask, and Watson with his revolver, and you tell them both that they are on no account to climb over. By nightfall they have found the barn that Stapleton uses as a kennel, and a smell of paint that will not wash.

echoes.text: You saw Stapleton's face by the dead man's side. You will know it again.
The label in the coat says Sir Henry Baskerville. The hound was sent for the wrong man, and the right man is alive.
The dead pony's throat was torn clean through, by a thing that stood up on its hind legs.
Dr Mortimer's chart of the Mire has a path pencilled across it that nobody else knows.
A line of white wands runs out into the Mire from the end of Merripit's pasture.
You ran to the cry, and arrived too late.
You counted the cellar keys on the nail, and Selden was asleep in the straw.
Stapleton has shaken your hand. It was as dry as paper.
Stapleton knows that you are on the moor, and has said so, with great politeness.
The shepherd has been asked to keep quiet, and the whole of Grimpen has heard the cry.

D26.title: Coombe Tracey
D26.description:
Monday 21 October 1889, noon. Laura Lyons lives in a pretty, shabby little house at the end of the single street, with a typewriter on the table in the window and a bunch of Michaelmas daisies in a jam-jar. She is a dark, handsome, tired woman of thirty, with a quick, nervous way of moving her hands.

She does not look pleased to see two strangers on her doorstep, and does not ask you to sit. It is her letter that Sir Charles had in his pocket, and she has not told the whole truth. She has been waiting for somebody to catch her at it for two months.

options.label: Tell Her Who Stapleton Is and What He Meant to Do to Her.
options.detail: A woman who has been used is angriest when she is told. She has been promised a divorce and a marriage, by someone who has a wife. It is a hard thing to hear, and she will hear it from you.

quote.speaker: Laura Lyons
quote.text: He told me that he would marry me, when I was free, and that Sir Charles would pay for the divorce. He dictated the note. He made me ask for the meeting at the gate, and then he told me not to go. I did not go.

success.outcome: She turns from you for a moment, and looks out of the window, and when she turns back her face is different. She does not weep. She says, in a flat, hard voice, that she will swear to it before any magistrate in Devon, and that she would like to be there when he is taken. You have the whole of it, in her own words, in a quarter of an hour.

failure.outcome: She is a proud woman, and it is the wrong thing to have said. She says that she has never in her life heard of a Mr Stapleton, and that you are impertinent, and that her father will hear of it. The door closes. You stand in the street with Watson, and the Michaelmas daisies in the window nod, and you have lost the best witness that you have.

options.label: Show Her Frankland's Letter and Ask for Her Side.
options.detail: A father who has not spoken to her for years has written eleven pages, and her name is in the fourth. It may soften her to know that someone has been thinking of her.

quote.speaker: Laura Lyons
quote.text: My father has been writing about me? Nobody in this county has said my name aloud in two years. He saw a gentleman at Merripit? Yes, I know who it was. I should like to tell somebody before it goes out of my head.

options.outcome: She sits down, and puts her hands over her face, and then takes them away and says that you had better have the whole of it. It is half a story, half a confession. She was lonely, and he was kind, and he was married, and she did not know. She says that she will think about swearing to it, and that you must give her a day.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs Frankland's letter about the gentleman at Merripit

options.label: Leave Her Alone and Watch Her House for the Evening.
options.detail: A woman who has been frightened will go to her protector. If she goes to Merripit, you will know where he is, and if she does not, you will know that he is not in the habit of it.
options.outcome: You sit in a hedge, with Watson, for three hours of rain, and see nothing that you could put before a court. It is the dull part of the work, and the part that no one writes about. At eleven the light goes out. You walk back to the moor in silence.

D26B.title: The Warrant
D26B.description: Tuesday 22 October 1889, ten in the morning. Laura Lyons has sworn her statement in the front room of her house, before a magistrate who has been got out of bed, in a clear, dry voice, with her hand on the book. It runs to four pages. Lestrade, who has come down by the night train, reads it standing, and goes red, and then white, and then puts it carefully in his pocket-book. There is a warrant by noon. There is a party of six constables by two. By four, Merripit House is surrounded, and the front door is open, and the master of it is sitting in the parlour with a book on his knee and a cup of tea at his elbow, waiting.

options.label: Go In by the Front Door and Take Stapleton Yourself.
options.detail: Anyone who sets a hound has to be faced before he is judged. He will say that he is innocent, and the room will say otherwise. It is the proper way to end a case, and you have not done it in months.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Jack Stapleton, alias Vandeleur, I arrest you on a charge of conspiracy to murder Sir Henry Baskerville. It is my duty to caution you that anything you say may be taken down.

options.outcome: He puts down his cup, and rises, and gives a small, formal bow. He is civil. He says that he is sorry that his wife is not at home, since she would have wished to say goodbye. He says it with a great deal of gentleness. There is no hound in the house. There is a bare wooden kennel in the barn, and a great black stain on the floor of it.

options.label: Let Lestrade Make the Arrest and Wait on the Road.
options.detail: Someone who is taken by the Yard is anyone who is taken properly, and the credit is the Yard's. It is a great deal less exciting than a night on the moor, and a great deal safer.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: You'll want to be out of it, Mr Holmes. I'll say I had the warrant from a lady in Coombe Tracey and a tip from London, and leave the rest to the Assizes.

options.outcome: You stand on the road with your hands in your pockets, and watch the constables go up the drive. It is a damp, cold, uneventful afternoon. The arrest takes four minutes, and there is no hound, and no scream, and no ghost. The papers will say that the Yard has taken a dangerous man. They will be right.

D27.title: The Last Preparations
D27.description: Wednesday 23 October 1889, in the afternoon. The plan has been made, and the day has been chosen, and a baronet has promised to dine at Merripit on Friday. The hut is full of maps and pencil-ends, and the stove smokes. You have forty-eight hours in which to do what you can, and you cannot do all of it. A hound must be met on a path, and a man must be kept alive on it. It is a plain, grim piece of arithmetic, and it will take the whole of what you have.

options.label: Meet Lestrade at Princetown and Bring His Men Up to the Moor.
options.detail: A body of trained men on a dark path is a safeguard that no one man, however clever, can supply. They must be taught to lie still, and not to fire until they are told.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Six of 'em, and a sergeant who's shot a mad dog. They'll be on the moor by Friday dusk, in their own clothes. I've never had such an odd job.

options.outcome: He shakes your hand with a gruff, awkward kindness, and the thing is settled. The Yard is a heavy, clumsy, trustworthy engine, and it has the one merit that you have never been able to supply: it does not tire.
options.requiresHint: Needs the men you asked Lestrade to hold

options.label: Wire Lestrade in London and Ask Him to Come Down at Once.
options.detail: A man who was not told to hold his men can still be sent for. It will cost you two days that you have not got, and plenty of the Yard's patience, and he will come, grumbling, by the night train.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: You want me on Dartmoor by Friday, Mr Holmes, with six men, on a hound? I'll come. I'll say that I'm inspecting the prison. They'll believe that, I daresay.

options.outcome: The answer is a single line, and you have never been so glad of an unwilling policeman. He comes down with six constables, a sergeant and a cold, and puts the whole of the Yard's grudging weight behind a thing that he does not in the least believe in.

options.label: Take Sir Henry into Your Confidence and Tell Him Everything.
options.detail: He is the man who will walk the path. A person who knows what is on it will walk it better than one who does not, and a brave man deserves to know why.

quote.speaker: Sir Henry Baskerville
quote.text: So the thing is real, Mr Holmes, and it was never the Baskerville curse. It was a man with a dog. I'm glad. I'd sooner fight a man than a ghost. I'll walk the path on Friday as if I'd been born to it.

options.outcome: He takes it, quietly, and goes white, and then asks for the facts in order. This is the most useful half-hour of the week. Sir Henry is not clever, but he is steady, and a steady man is worth a hundred who are brilliant on the night.

options.label: Spend the Day on the Mire with the Wand Marks and a Rope.
options.detail: A path across a bog is not the same thing in the dark. If a man runs, he runs along it, and a rope and a lamp at the edge may be the difference between a prisoner and a corpse.
options.outcome: You go out in the grey afternoon with a coil of rope and a long pole, and walk the whole of the line, and come back with your boots black to the knee. You have had no company but the curlews. By dusk you have a map of the one road that is safe, and a sick feeling that it is the only thing that you have been sure of all week.

echoes.text: Laura Lyons has shut her door on you, and you have no one to say that the note was dictated.
She told you half, and has promised the rest on Thursday. You do not think that you will have the time.
Lestrade is waiting for Laura Lyons's sworn statement, which has not come.
Watson and Cartwright have watched the barn at Merripit, which smells of paint.
You watched Laura Lyons's house for three hours of rain, and saw a gate open once at nine.

D28.title: The Fog
D28.description: Friday 25 October 1889, ten at night. A white fog has come up from the Mire in the last hour, and the whole of the moor is blotted out. You are lying in a hollow of the heather two hundred yards from the gate of Merripit House, where the path from the house joins the road to the Hall. The only light in the world is the yellow square of the dining-room window. Sir Henry is inside, and will come out in an hour, and walk home. The fog lies on the heather like wet wool. There is no sound, and no wind, and you are cold.

options.label: Put Lestrade's Men Where the Beast Will Not Scent Them.
options.detail: A hound hunts by the nose, and a nose can be fooled by the wind. The men must lie to leeward of the path, in the heather, with their lamps shut.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Four in the heather to the north of the path, and two at the gate. They'll lie like stones, Mr Holmes. I've told them that anyone who coughs goes home on the next train.

options.outcome: They go to ground in the dusk, one at a time, with their coats turned and their boots tied with sacking. In ten minutes the moor is as empty as it was at noon. You know where each of them is, and you cannot see one.
options.requiresHint: Needs Lestrade's men on the moor

options.label: Keep Watson Beside You in the Hollow.
options.detail: He has a revolver, a steady hand and an excellent sense of what to do in the dark. He will do exactly as he is told, which is more than can be said of most heroes.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I am here, Holmes. I have been badly frightened on this moor, and I have never been so glad of anything as of your voice. Tell me when, and I shall fire.

options.outcome: He crouches in the heather at your left shoulder, with his hat pulled down and the revolver on his knee. You can hear him breathing, quietly and steadily, as he did in the second Afghan war. You put out your hand and touch his sleeve.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs Watson to know that you are on the moor

options.label: Wait Alone Where the Path Bends.
options.detail: A man alone makes the smallest sound and leaves the least scent. This is the best way to see, and the worst way to act.
options.outcome: You lie down in a hollow of the turf, with your face in the heather and your pistol under your hand. The cold comes up through the ground. You think of the hut, and of the stove in it, and of London, and you put each of them out of your mind in turn.

echoes.text: Sir Henry knows what is on the path, and has gone to dinner with his pistol in his pocket and a smile on his face.
The wands go into the Mire from the end of the pasture. In this fog they will be invisible, and you have the line of them in your head.
You asked a brave man to walk home alone across the moor. It is the thing that you are least proud of in all your life.

D29.title: The Hound
D29.description:
Friday 25 October 1889, a little before eleven. The door of Merripit House opens, and a figure with a stick comes out into the lamplight, and says good night to somebody inside. It is Sir Henry, in his brown ulster. He sets off along the path with a firm tread, and the fog closes behind him.

A hundred yards behind him, at the far edge of the pasture, a pale light springs up and begins to move. It is low, and steady, and keeps pace with the baronet, and a little way behind it comes a sound that you will not be able to describe to anybody afterwards: a long, deep, rolling bay.

options.label: Fire at the Beast as It Springs.
options.detail: A mastiff-hound with a coat of phosphorus is an animal that can be killed, if it can be hit. It is a matter of the first second, and of a steady hand.

quote.speaker: Sir Henry Baskerville
quote.text: God in heaven! Holmes, Holmes, there it is! It's the size of a calf, and it's on fire! I can't see it. Where is it? For God's sake, shoot!

success.outcome: It comes out of the fog in a single bound, with its jaws open and the light streaming from its mouth, and you put five bullets into it before it reaches the path. It goes down on its side with a howl that you will remember to the end of your days. Sir Henry is on his back in the heather, white as paper and untouched, and the great pale creature is lying across his legs.

failure.outcome: The fog and the glare make it a bad mark, and the first shot goes wide. The second, you think, hits. The beast does not stop. It goes over the baronet like a wave, and he is down, with the great jaws at his throat and the light running along his sleeve. For an instant the whole of the world is a screaming, flickering, deafening muddle, and you have the horrid conviction that you are too late.

options.label: Let Lestrade's Men Rise and Shoot Together.
options.detail: Six men with rifles on a dark path can fire a volley that no single hand can match. It is the job that they were brought for, and it is one that no roll should decide.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Now, lads! Fire! And God help us if it isn't what he says it is! That's the beast. That's the thing, and it's gone for the gentleman. Take it low!

options.outcome: They come up out of the heather like men out of a grave, and the volley is a flat, hard, enormous noise that rolls away across the Mire. The hound stops, and turns in the air, and comes down on its back with its legs thrashing. Sir Henry has not been touched. He is sitting in the heather with his face in his hands, and he is laughing, and he is crying.
options.requiresHint: Needs Lestrade's men hidden along the path

options.label: Stand Between the Beast and Sir Henry and Show It a Lamp.
options.detail: A creature that has been painted with phosphorus is a creature of flesh. If it is known to be mortal, it can be faced, and a lamp is a thing that any dog will shy at.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: It is a dog, and it has been painted. It will not stop for a lamp, but it will for a pistol. I must keep my head, and hit it on the first bound, or the second. It is a large dog.

options.requiresFlagHint: Needs the smell of phosphorus, from the pony or the barn

success.outcome: You take your stand in the path with the lamp in your left hand and the pistol in your right, and the beast comes out of the fog with the brightness of a falling star. You wait for it with a calm that you have not felt all week. Four shots, close together, and it goes down at your feet in a heap of black hair and white fire.

failure.outcome: The lamp goes out under the beast's first touch. You fire, and the light dances, and you cannot tell whether it is the creature or the fog that you have hit. It goes past you with a rush and a smell of burning, and you hear Sir Henry cry out behind you in the dark.

echoes.text: Watson is beside you in the heather, with his hand on your sleeve, and he has stopped breathing.
The moor is quiet. You know that ten men are lying along the path, with their rifles ready, and not one of them can be heard.
You are alone in the heather, and nobody can see you, or help.

D30.title: The Second Chance
D30.description: A second later. Sir Henry is on his back in the heather with the great beast on his chest, and its jaws are a hand's breadth from his face. The phosphorus is running down its flanks in a pale stream, and in the fog it is terrible and absurd, like a bad painting of Hell. He is shouting, and then he is not. You have your pistol in your hand and a single clear second in which to use it, and every thing in the world depends upon whether you can be trusted with it.

options.label: Put the Muzzle to Its Ear and Fire.
options.detail: Anyone who must shoot at a dog on a man's chest has one place to aim at, and it is the place where a bullet cannot go on. It is the hardest shot that you have ever had to make.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: I have fired at a good many things in my life. I have not often been so sure that I should miss.

success.outcome: The muzzle is touching the hair behind its ear, and you fire, and it is over. The great body jerks, and rolls, and lies still. Sir Henry is lying under it with his mouth open and his eyes shut, and you drag it off him with your two hands. He is alive. He is alive, and his throat is not touched, and the light has gone out of the beast like a candle.

failure.outcome: You are a half-second late, and the beast has turned its head. The bullet goes through its shoulder, and the jaws close. Sir Henry gives one cry and then none. When you have pulled the dead hound away he is lying with his throat torn open and his hands still clutching at the heather, and the last of the light is going out of his eyes. You have come, once in your life, a minute too late.

options.label: Call to Watson to Fire from the Left.
options.detail: A second gun, on the other side, is a thing that a beast cannot turn on at once. Watson is a surgeon, a soldier and a good shot.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I have it, Holmes. It is a ugly thing to have to do to an animal. It is a worse thing to have not done.

options.requiresFlagHint: Needs Watson beside you in the hollow

success.outcome: He fires twice, steadily, from the left, and the great head jerks and drops. Sir Henry rolls clear, with his coat in ribbons and his shoulder bloody, and Watson is on his knees beside him with his bag. It is the surest shot that you have ever seen him make. He says, calmly, that the arm will mend, and that he would like a cigarette.

failure.outcome: The second shot goes through the beast's neck, and kills it, and the first has gone through Sir Henry's sleeve. He lies in the heather with an arm that is full of blood and a face that is empty. He is alive, and he will live. But he is not looking at you, or at anything, and when Watson takes his hand, he does not know it.

options.label: Whistle for the Men in the Heather.
options.detail: A volley has the weight of ten men's nerve, and a beast that is shot by a dozen is a beast that is dead. It is the one thing that can be done in a second, and it may be enough.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: It's on him! Fire, boys, fire! Take it low! For God's sake, don't hit the gentleman! That's it. That's the way. Hold it. Hold it. It's down.

options.outcome: The rifles go off, one after another, in the dark. It is a long, ragged, terrible second. When the smoke clears the hound is a heap of stinking hair on the path. Sir Henry, with his coat torn from collar to hem, is being pulled to his feet by two constables and a sergeant who has never in his life been so pleased with himself.
options.requiresHint: Needs Lestrade's men hidden along the path

D31.title: The Mire
D31.description: A little after eleven. The beast is dead, and Sir Henry is alive, and you leave him with Watson and run. There is a figure in the pasture, in the fog, a hundred yards away: a thin man in a long coat. He has been standing at the edge of the path with a lantern, and he is now running for the Mire. He knows the way. He does not run like a person who is afraid. He runs like someone who has a road to a place, and who has not often had to hurry. In half a minute he will be on the line of white wands, and then the fog will have him.

options.label: Follow Him Along the Line of the Wands.
options.detail: A path that a man knows in the dark is a path that another may follow in the light. It is a thing that you have walked, and he has not known it.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs the line of white wands, walked by daylight

success.outcome: You go out along the line at a run, with your eyes on the lantern ahead, and you count the wands as you pass. At the fifth he turns to the left, as he must, and you turn to the right, and when he stops, panting, at the end of the firm ground, you are at his elbow with a pistol. He stares at you with an expression of the purest surprise. He has never known that he could be followed.

failure.outcome: The fog is thicker than you had thought, and the third wand has been moved. You step off the firm ground, and the black water takes you to the thigh, and you cling to a tussock with both hands while the lantern ahead of you goes out among the reeds. By the time that Watson has dragged you back to the path the man has gone, and the Mire has closed over the place where he was.

options.label: Let Lestrade's Men Take Him on the Pasture Side.
options.detail: Someone who runs for a Mire can be cut off from the road, and Lestrade's men are in the heather already. It is a plain bit of police work, and it is the only way to be sure.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Round the north side, lads, and cut him off at the gate! He'll not go far in that fog. We'll have him on the road in two minutes, or I'll eat my hat.

options.outcome: They go off at a run, with their lamps unshuttered, and the thin figure ahead of them stops, and looks back, and sees ten men coming across the pasture. For an instant he stands still. Then he turns, and lifts his hands, with a gesture of weary courtesy, as if he had lost a game of chess.
options.requiresHint: Needs Lestrade's men hidden along the path

options.label: Let the Mire Have Him and Go Back to Sir Henry.
options.detail: A person who runs into a bog in a fog on a dark night has chosen where he will die. It is not a hanging, and it is not an escape. It is the moor's own justice.
options.outcome: You stand at the edge of the pasture, with the fog on your face, and listen to a cry in the dark that is first a call and then a cry and then a long, thin, falling note that stops. It is a sound that you have heard before. You do not turn your head, and you do not follow. That is the first time in your life that you have let a criminal go.

echoes.text: The rifles went off together, and the echo is still rolling over the Mire.

D32.title: Merripit House
D32.description:
Friday 25 October 1889, past midnight. The door of Merripit House is open, and a lamp is burning in the hall. The rooms are as neat as a schoolmaster's. There is a butterfly cabinet in the parlour, and a row of books about moths, and in the upper room at the back, tied to a post with strips of a sheet, a woman who is gagged and white.

She looks at you with eyes in which there is no surprise whatever. She is the wife of the man in the Mire, and has been the sister of him since the day that they came to Devon. She has been waiting for somebody for four years.

options.label: Cut Her Free and Ask for Her Word.
options.detail: A woman who has been tied to a post by her husband is a witness of a particular kind. She will say what she has seen, if she is asked kindly and not hurried, and if the man is out of the house.

quote.speaker: Mrs Stapleton
quote.text: He is not my brother, Mr Holmes, and he never was. I have known it since the day that we were married. I will tell you everything, and you will be shocked, and I shall not mind. I should like to be believed.

options.outcome: She tells it in a low, steady voice, over a cup of tea at the kitchen table, with Watson at the door. It takes two hours. It is the whole history of a clever, patient, joyless man. At the end she says that she is tired, and that she would like to go to bed, and that she has not slept for four years.

options.label: Search the Barn for the Kennel and the Pot of Paint.
options.detail: A hound has to be kept somewhere, and anyone who paints it has the means in a tin. A court will want the tin, and the chain, and the dish.
options.outcome: You go through the barn in half an hour with a lantern. It is as bare and clean as the rest of the house. There is a straw bed, a chain, a dish with a name on it that has been scratched out, and in a corner a stone jar with a label that says, in a neat hand, Phosphorus. It is the thing that you came for.

options.label: Leave Her to the Doctor and Go Out to Look for Him.
options.detail: A woman who has been gagged and tied wants a physician and not a policeman, and the man who has done it is still out on the moor. It is a harsh, practical, unjust choice.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are right, I suppose. I shall stay with her, and give her a sedative. You had better go, if you are going. I do not think that you will find him.

options.outcome: You leave her with Watson and a lamp. The moor is as silent as a church. You spend an hour with a lantern at the edge of the pasture, and you hear nothing, and see nothing, and come back with your hands cold.

echoes.text: He is in the lock-up at Grimpen, with a constable at the door, drinking a cup of tea. He has asked politely whether his wife is well.
The Mire has closed over him, and nothing has risen.
The fog has closed over the place where you went in, and your boots are black to the thigh.

D33.title: A Retrospection
D33.description: Saturday 26 October 1889, noon. The sun has come out at last, and the moor is a great brown and purple bowl of light, and the hut is the one thing on it that is out of place. Sir Henry is in bed at the Hall with an arm in a sling, and Dr Mortimer in the room with a bottle. Lestrade has gone to Princetown. Watson is writing, with a sheet of foolscap on his knee, and the sentence at the head of it is the first of a long account. You have a day in which to say what is to be said, and to whom.

options.label: Say That the Mire Keeps Its Own and Close the Case.
options.detail: Anyone who has been sucked into a bog is a person who has been tried, and there is no appeal. It is a clean, plain, unlawful end, and it spares a good many people.

quote.speaker: Dr Mortimer
quote.text: I shall say that it was a misadventure, Mr Holmes, and I shall sign the certificate. The Baskerville curse will have a new chapter. I am only sorry that it has an end.

options.outcome: He says it with a long, sad smile, and signs. The county will say that old Hugo has been revenged. A paragraph in the Western Morning News will say that a naturalist has been lost in the Mire. You send a note to Lestrade, and he writes back that he is a great deal relieved.
options.requiresHint: Needs the Mire to have taken him

options.label: Take Stapleton to the Assizes and Let the Law Hear It.
options.detail: Someone who has been taken alive has to be tried, and a trial has to have evidence. It will be a long autumn in Exeter, and a satisfying one.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: He's in the cells at Exeter, Mr Holmes, and he's been civil. I've got the dealer, the schoolmaster and the kennel. It'll be a long trial and a clean one.

options.outcome: He grins, and slaps your arm. It is the plainest, most satisfying piece of work that you have been associated with for a year. The Assizes will sit in November, and the verdict will be that the prisoner is guilty of conspiracy and attempted murder, and that he is not insane. It will not need a ghost.
options.requiresHint: Needs him taken, and evidence that would hold at the Assizes

options.label: Let His Wife Speak for Herself at the Trial.
options.detail: A woman who has been the instrument of a murderer's plans and the victim of his temper has a right to be heard. It will cost her a great deal to say it, and it may spare her a great deal more.

quote.speaker: Mrs Stapleton
quote.text: I should like to say what I have said to you, Mr Holmes, in a court, in front of him. I have been afraid of him for four years. I should like to see whether I can stop.

options.outcome: She stands in the dock at Exeter in a plain black dress, and speaks for an hour, in a low, clear voice, without notes. The judge, who is an old man, takes his spectacles off. When she has done, the jury does not retire. It is the finest piece of testimony that you have ever heard, and you were not allowed to say a word of it.
options.requiresHint: Needs him taken, and his wife to have spoken

options.label: Ask the Home Office to Remember the Convict Who Was Kept Safe.
options.detail: A person who was hidden in a cellar, and not sent out on the moor in a baronet's coat, has a right to a little leniency. It is a small thing to ask, and it may be a large one to grant.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: The Home Office will, I think, listen to a good report of a prisoner who gave himself up and did no harm. I shall write to the Secretary. It is not a reprieve, Sherlock, but it is not a rope.

options.outcome: Your brother writes, and the Home Secretary reads, and the thing is done in a fortnight. A convict who was eight years in Princetown goes back to it in a quiet van, and will not be hanged. Barrymore's wife has a letter, once a month, from a chaplain, and says it is the only post that she has ever been glad of.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs Selden kept in the cellar at the Hall

options.label: Leave the Rest to the County Police and Go Home to London.
options.detail: A hound is dead, and a baronet is alive, and the case that was set you has been done. The rest is for the magistrates, and you have never in your life enjoyed the aftermath.
options.outcome: You take the evening train, with a second-class ticket and a clear conscience, and in the third week of November the papers say that the county police have not been able to find the naturalist of Merripit. His wife has gone to her relations. The hound is buried in a field.

echoes.text: The hound lies in the Grimpen lock-up, with a tarpaulin over it, waiting for a coroner. It is the size of a calf.
Sir Henry has said that he is well. It is a thing that he has said four times, and he has gone a little whiter on each.
The kennel, the chain and the pot of phosphorus are in the barn, and Lestrade has counted them.
You left Mrs Stapleton to the doctor, and you have not forgiven yourself.

P1.title: The Doctor from Lauder
P1.description: Tuesday 4 January 1887, a bitter morning with the fog down to the area railings. A Scottish doctor in a black coat is sitting on the edge of the basket-chair with his hat between his knees. He has come three hundred miles to say a thing that he cannot prove. Dr Rennie of Lauder attended Mrs Stewart, a widow of seventy, who died last week in her bed of what the nephew says was a failure of the heart. The doctor was told so, and signed. He has not slept since. There was nothing in the room, he says, and nothing in the glass, and yet he knows that somebody has been there.

options.label: Ask for the Last Prescription and the Certificate.
options.detail: A doctor who is afraid has kept his papers. A prescription says what was given, and a certificate says what he was told to say.

quote.speaker: Dr Rennie
quote.text: There is nothing in the bottle but what I ordered, Mr Holmes, and I have had it analysed. It is the cleanest bottle in Berwickshire. That is what frightens me. A poison would have been a comfort.

options.outcome: He puts the papers on the table with a shaking hand. You read them through, and find nothing. It is a perfect death, as clean as a sum, and a doctor who has been robbed of his fear of a poisoner is a doctor who is left with his fear of a man.

options.label: Ask Who Nursed Her at the End.
options.detail: A woman of seventy does not die alone. Somebody was in the house, and somebody has since left it.

quote.speaker: Dr Rennie
quote.text: A Mrs Dunbar, from an agency in Edinburgh, who had the best of testimonials. She was a quiet, capable person. She left on the morning after the funeral, and I have not been able to find her since.

options.outcome: He gives you the name of the agency, and you write it down. A nurse who has the best of testimonials and cannot be found is a nurse who has done something, or had something done to her. You put a question mark against her name that is as long as the page.

options.label: Ask Who Gains by the Death.
options.detail: A widow of seventy has a house, and a house has an heir. It is the commonest question in the world, and the one that is least often asked in time.

quote.speaker: Dr Rennie
quote.text: A nephew in London, a Mr Stewart, who has taken the whole of it, and left for the Continent the day of the funeral. A pleasant young man. He wept at the grave. I do not think that he was acting, and I do not think that he was grieving.

options.outcome: You say that you will come to Lauder tomorrow. He goes grey with relief, and shakes your hand in both of his. It is the whole of his stock of courage that he has laid on your table, and you feel it, like a coin, in your pocket.

P2.title: Lauder
P2.description: Wednesday 5 January 1887, noon. The house at Lauder is tall, grey and shut, with a gravel sweep and a monkey-puzzle tree, and a maid at the door who has been crying. It is cold in every room. The bed in which Mrs Stewart died has been stripped. The nurse's room, at the end of the passage, has been turned out as thoroughly as a room can be that has been left by a woman in a hurry. There is a drawer in a chest, with a few papers in it, and the maid says that she has been told not to touch them.

options.label: Read the Nurse's Testimonial in the Drawer.
options.detail: A woman with the best of testimonials will have kept them, and a testimonial is signed. It is a small piece of paper, and it has a large name on it.
options.outcome: It is not a name that you know. It is a fine, firm, schoolmaster's signature, and a letter that is as cold as a sum. You put it in your pocket-book without a word, and note that someone who gives a testimonial to a nurse in Edinburgh does not usually sign himself with his degree.

options.label: Walk the Garden and the Wall.
options.detail: A house with a tall wall and a gate has had visitors. They will have left their mark on the gravel, or the lane beyond it.

quote.speaker: The gardener
quote.text: A cab, sir, in the lane, the night before she died, and the one before. Not a Lauder cab. A town one, with a lamp that was a bit crooked. It waited an hour, and went. I told Dr Rennie, and he said that it was no business of ours.

options.outcome: You walk the lane for a quarter of a mile with your eyes on the ground, and find, in the wet, the print of a wheel and the stub of a good cigar. Anyone who waits an hour in a cab, in the cold, is anyone who is paid to. It will not take you to the nurse, or to the nephew. It may take you to a cab-yard.

options.label: Sit with the Maid in the Kitchen.
options.detail: A maid has eyes and ears in a house, and a shut mouth in front of the master. She will talk to a stranger who gives her tea and no advice.

quote.speaker: The maid
quote.text: There was a tall gentleman came to the house, sir, a week before. He said he was the nurse's brother. He had a tall hat, and he never took it off. I thought he'd the look of a clergyman. The mistress was taken with him.

options.outcome: She cries a little, and drinks her tea. A gentleman with a hat, a brother who is not a brother, and a mistress who was taken. It is the weakest evidence in the world, and it is a description, and nobody has asked you for one. You write it down in the kitchen, with the tea going cold.

echoes.text: Mrs Dunbar was sent by an agency in Edinburgh. The agency's secretary has said that she has never heard of her.

P3.title: The Clerk in the River
P3.description:
Monday 10 January 1887, the early morning. A man is lying on the stairs of Blackfriars Pier with the water running out of his coat, and a constable standing over him with a lantern. He is a thin, grey, tidy man of fifty, in a clerk's black, and he has been in the river for two nights.

In his pocket is a season ticket, a pawn-ticket and a letter to his wife that has not been posted. He was a senior clerk at the bank of Cowley and Vane, in Lombard Street, and nobody has said a word against him. The Yard has called it a suicide. Inspector Lestrade has called it a puzzle, and sent for you.

options.label: Read the Unposted Letter to His Wife.
options.detail: Someone who is going to kill himself writes a letter that says so. A person who is going to be killed writes a letter that says nothing at all, and is the more interesting.
options.outcome: You read it twice. It is a plain, kind, flustered little note, and it is not the letter of a person who means to die. It is the letter of someone who has been told to go to a meeting, and who has gone, and who will be late.

options.label: Look at the Pawn-Ticket and Ask What He Pledged.
options.detail: A clerk of fifty who pawns a thing is a clerk who is short of money, and anyone who is short of money may be bought. It is the oldest of motives.
options.outcome: You take the ticket to the shop in the Borough. The pawnbroker remembers him, and says that he was ashamed, and that a man in a tall hat had waited for him on the other side of the street. It is the second tall hat in a week. You do not think that it is the same man, and you do not think that it is a different one.

options.label: Ask Lestrade to Hold the Body and the Case Open.
options.detail: A verdict of suicide closes a file, and a file that is closed is a file that nobody will reopen. It is a small, civil, bureaucratic thing to ask, and it is the most important.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I'll hold it a week, Mr Holmes, and say the coroner's busy. But if you've got nothing by then, I'll have to let it go as it stands.

options.outcome: He is not a person who is easily moved. He writes a note for the coroner, and a second for the sergeant. It is the beginning of a long friendship, and neither of you knows it. You walk away from the pier with the river smell in your coat and the sense of a case that has begun to grow a second head.

P4.title: The Altered Ledger
P4.description: Tuesday 11 January 1887, the forenoon. The bank of Cowley and Vane is a narrow, dark, polite house in Lombard Street, with a row of high desks and a smell of ink and gas. The manager is a plump, anxious gentleman called Mr Vane, who has been told by the Yard that his dead clerk is a puzzle, and has decided that it is a scandal. He takes you into his room, and closes the door. There is a ledger on his table. It is open at the page that was Mr Alcott's, and a sum on it has been altered by a good hand.

options.label: Look at the Altered Figure and the Hand That Made It.
options.detail: A forger leaves his own hand under the one that he is copying. It is in the loops, and in the way that the pen is lifted, and it will be the same on any other paper.
options.outcome: You hold the ledger to the window for a long time. This is the first moment of real alarm that you have felt in the case. A name that has appeared on a nurse's testimonial in Scotland has appeared again on a bond in the City.

options.label: Ask Who Else Had the Key to the Strong-Room.
options.detail: A bank has a short list of men who can alter a ledger. It is a matter of three or four faces, and you will know the one by his answer.

quote.speaker: Mr Vane
quote.text: Three of us, Mr Holmes. Myself, the dead man and a Mr Brandon, who is a clerk of the greatest probity. I do not wish to say a word against him. He has been with us for six years. He has not been to the office since Thursday.

options.outcome: He gives you the name, and you give it to Lestrade. It will turn out in a week that Mr Brandon is in Brighton with a nervous breakdown, and that he had been told that his mother was dying. It is a thing that happens when a man is not allowed to ask.

options.label: Say That the Bank Must Keep Its Own Counsel and Tell No One.
options.detail: A manager who is told that the matter is serious will be silent. A manager who is silent will not tell the newspapers, and a newspaper may warn the man who did it.

quote.speaker: Mr Vane
quote.text: I am only too glad, Mr Holmes. I have not told a soul. I have kept it from my partner, my wife and my cat. That is the most dreadful piece of business that the house has known since the Overend Gurney failure.

options.outcome: He shakes your hand with great warmth, and you leave with a sense of a bank that has done as it was told. It is not a clue, and it is a courtesy, and you have learned that a quiet bank is better than a talkative one. You do not look at the ledger again. You have not, you tell yourself, had a good enough look.

P5.title: The Empty Study
P5.description: Monday 17 January 1887, noon. A study in Kensington has been broken into by somebody who took nothing. Dr Pell is an astronomer, a retired professor with a long white beard and a small house. He stands in the middle of his room in a dressing-gown with his hands behind his back and says that it is a most interesting phenomenon. Every drawer has been opened and every paper moved by an inch. Nothing is gone, and everything has been read. The lock of the door has not been forced. The only mark is a pale smear of chalk on the sill of the window.

options.label: Ask Whether He Has Lately Written Anything That Another Man Would Want.
options.detail: Anyone who burgles a study and takes nothing has been looking for something that he did not find, or something that he could copy. A man of science has no valuables but his ideas.

quote.speaker: Dr Pell
quote.text: A paper on the perturbations of the planetoids, Mr Holmes, which I read before the Society in November. A dull paper. A man at the back asked the only intelligent question that I have ever been asked. He gave his name as a Professor from the provinces.

options.outcome: He smiles in a pleased, vague way, and takes down a copy. It is a dry, close, mathematical work. You read the first page with some difficulty, and see why the questioner would have stood out. You write down the date, and the hall.

options.label: Look at the Chalk on the Window-Sill.
options.detail: A pale chalk smear on a sill is a mark that a burglar makes, to say that a house has been done or is to be done. It is also a mark that a teacher makes, by habit.
options.outcome: You put a pinch of it in an envelope, and Dr Pell looks at you with the tolerant interest of anyone who has seen a great many things done with a lens. A thief who is a schoolmaster is a pretty problem, and you carry it out of the house as a dog carries a bone.

options.label: Ask Who Else Has Been in the House This Month.
options.detail: A study that was entered without force was entered by a key, or by a door that was opened. The astronomer's housekeeper will know who came, and who did not give a name.

quote.speaker: Dr Pell
quote.text: Nobody, my dear sir. Nobody at all. A man came about the gas. A boy brought a note. And the secretary of the Society called, with a list of subscribers, to ask whether I should like my name left out of the printed volume. I said that I should not.

options.outcome: It is the mildest, most helpless of answers, and you make a note of each caller. The man from the gas, the boy with the note, and the secretary. He has been burgled in the most polite way, by somebody who was in no hurry. You do not like the sound of the third.

P6.title: The Subscribers' List
P6.description: Tuesday 18 January 1887, the afternoon. The Society of Mathematical and Astronomical Inquiry has two rooms above a printer's in Fetter Lane, and a secretary called Mr Garrod who is a great deal younger than his own beard. He is polite about the whole business and does not know what it is about. The printed volume of the papers is on his table, and at the back of it is a list of the subscribers, a hundred and forty names in a small, close type. He has a copy for you. He says that it is not a secret.

options.label: Read the List for Any Name That You Have Seen Before.
options.detail: A list of a hundred and forty names has one that is out of place, if you know what a place is. It is the work of a quarter of an hour, with a pencil, and the other thing is patience.
options.outcome: You go down the list with your pencil, and stop at the M's. Mr Garrod, who has been talking, stops too. It is an ordinary, harmless, learned subscription, and the name has been given to a printer in a entirely regular way. It is, you think, the most careful signature in London.

options.label: Ask Mr Garrod Who Asked About Dr Pell's Paper.
options.detail: A secretary knows who has written for a copy of a paper, and who has come to hear it. He will not remember a name, but he will remember a request.

quote.speaker: Mr Garrod
quote.text: A gentleman wrote for the paper in December, sir, and I sent it. A gentleman who said that he was a retired schoolmaster and had been working on the same problem for years. I thought it an agreeable letter. It is in the file.

options.outcome: He finds it, and you read it. It is dated from a lodging-house in Kensington, in a neat, even hand, and asks politely for a copy. It is signed with an initial only, and you copy the address. By the time that you arrive the lodging-house will have a new tenant.

options.label: Thank Him and Say That the Matter Is of No Importance.
options.detail: A person who has been asked a great many questions and sees that nothing has come of them is a person who is relieved. Relief is quiet, and a quiet secretary is a good one.

quote.speaker: Mr Garrod
quote.text: I am glad of it, Mr Holmes. I should not like the Society to get into the newspapers. We have always been so careful. Please do tell Dr Pell that his paper was a great success, and that nobody has asked for a refund.

options.outcome: You shake his hand, and take your copy of the list, and go out into Fetter Lane with a feeling of having done something clever and small. It is a dull way to spend an afternoon. You may be wrong. You do not think that you are.

P7.title: The Vanished Cabman
P7.description: Monday 24 January 1887, the morning. A forger has been tried at the Old Bailey, and acquitted, because the one witness who could have put him in the dock did not appear. He was a cabman, a respectable, steady old driver called Hobbs, who had taken the forger to a bank in the City on the day of the crime, and who had said so to the Yard. He left his house on the morning of the trial, in his Sunday coat, with his badge, and was not seen again. His wife has come to Baker Street. She has not taken off her bonnet, and she does not cry.

options.label: Ask Where He Was Last Seen and by Whom.
options.detail: Anyone who disappears has gone somewhere. Somebody has seen him go, and it is a matter of finding the one who has not been asked.

quote.speaker: Mrs Hobbs
quote.text: At the corner of our street, sir, with a gentleman. A tall gentleman in a good coat, who took his arm. My neighbour saw it. He thought it was a friend of his from the yard. He had a tall hat, and he was polite.

options.outcome: She says it in a flat, even voice, and sits down. It is the third gentleman in a tall hat since the beginning of January, and you do not like it. You say that you will find her husband, and she looks at you with a steady, tired contempt. She has been told a good many things by a good many gentlemen.

options.label: Ask Who Owns His Cab and Where It Stands.
options.detail: A cabman is a servant of a yard, and a yard has books. If he was bought, it was by someone who knew his habits, and a yard-master will be unable to say that he does not.
options.outcome: You put the name down, and underline the windfall. The yard-master is going to say that he has been fortunate, and that he has never heard of a gentleman in a tall hat. He will say it with a face like a plate. That is the first time that anyone has been so careful, and you suspect that the carefulness has been paid for.

options.label: Tell Mrs Hobbs That You Will Look for Him and Take Her Address.
options.detail: A woman who has been told that something will be done is a woman who can be left. It is a small, kind, necessary thing, and it will make no difference to the case.

quote.speaker: Mrs Hobbs
quote.text: I'll not be thanking you, sir, till he's home. But I'll say that you're the first gentleman who's asked me what he was like. It was always what he had done.

options.outcome: She takes your hand, briefly, with a hard, dry, grateful grasp. It is not the sort of thing that is written in the reports. A cab-driver of nineteen years' standing has left a woman who sits upright on a chair in a bonnet, and you cannot let the matter go.

P8.title: The Reference
P8.description: Tuesday 25 January 1887, noon. The forger who walked out of the Old Bailey is a mild, grey, cheerful person called Gilbert Crane, who lives in a villa in Clapham with a canary. He has been acquitted, and has no objection to being asked how. He sits in his arm-chair and looks at you over his spectacles, with the gentleness of anyone who has been told by experts that he is innocent. His solicitor's papers are on the table. His defence rested on a character reference, and it was that, you learn, which was thought to have moved the jury.

options.label: Ask to See the Reference That Was Read to the Jury.
options.detail: A character reference is a letter, and a letter is signed. A forger who has a referee of high standing has a friend, or he has been given one.

quote.speaker: Gilbert Crane
quote.text: A most flattering one, Mr Holmes, from a Professor of mathematics whom I have never had the honour to meet. I was astonished when it arrived. It said that I was a man of the strictest probity. I have it framed.

options.outcome: He takes it down from the wall, and you read it in the light of the window. It is signed J. Moriarty, in the same firm copperplate. A man whom he has never met has given him a character, and a jury has believed it. It is the fourth time that the name has been written, and it is, you see, the first time that it has done anyone any good.

options.label: Ask How the Witness Came to Be Absent.
options.detail: A person who is acquitted for want of a witness has been fortunate, or has had a friend. He may have been told, or he may have guessed. It is a question of manner, and he has none.

quote.speaker: Gilbert Crane
quote.text: I am told that the poor fellow had a bad turn, Mr Holmes. I do hope that he is better. I sent him a ham. It is the sort of thing that a man like myself does, when he has been so well treated by the world.

options.outcome: He says it with a vague, cheerful sweetness, and offers you a cup of tea. It is wholly plain that he has no notion of what has been done for him. He is a person who has been used, and has no idea of it, and you leave the villa with the canary singing behind you and a cold feeling in the stomach.

options.label: Tell Him That He Has Been Very Lucky and Leave It There.
options.detail: Anyone who is told that he is lucky will say so to his friends. Someone who has a friend will tell him, and the friend will want to know who has been asking.

quote.speaker: Gilbert Crane
quote.text: Lucky, Mr Holmes? I am told that it is a gift. I have always been a lucky man. I shall tell my solicitor that you called, and that you were most civil. I think that he will be pleased.

options.outcome: He beams at you, and you wish that you had not said it. A person who passes on a remark is someone who tells a friend, and a friend is a thing that you have been trying to avoid for three weeks. You go out into the road with a sense of having done a stupid thing, and of having done it slowly.

P9.title: The Board
P9.description:
Monday 31 January 1887, ten at night. The wall of the sitting-room at 221B has been cleared, and in a month it has been covered. A widow in Lauder, a clerk in the river, an astronomer's study and a vanished cabman have each a card in the middle of a sheet of brown paper, with strings and pins and a hundred notes in three kinds of ink.

Watson has gone to bed. The lamp is turned low, and you are standing in front of it with your hands behind your back. Four cases, in a month, in four parts of England, and every one of them a little too clean. You have a feeling about the wall that you have not had before. It is that someone has arranged it for you.

options.label: Lay the Names Side by Side.
options.detail: A forger varies his hand, and anyone who writes four testimonials in a week writes the same loop in each. It wants a lens, a patient mind and the courage to believe the lens.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: J. Moriarty, M.A., on a nurse's testimonial in Lauder. J. Moriarty, guarantor, on a bond in Lombard Street. Moriarty, Prof. J., on a list of subscribers in Fetter Lane. Three towns, three papers, three crimes. One loop in the J.

options.outcome: You step back from the wall, and the whole of it comes to you at once, with the strange, soft clearness of a thing that has been in front of you all the time. It is not a pattern of crimes. It is a pattern of a signature. Anyone who commits a murder, and a bank fraud, and a burglary, and a bribe, and signs all four, is a person who does not believe in being caught.
options.requiresHint: Needs the name in three of the four cases

options.label: Follow the Cab-Yard in Southwark.
options.detail: A cab at the gate in Lauder, a cabman gone in London and a yard-master with a new roof. This is the only thread that runs through the whole of the wall, and it is a thread that you can touch.
options.outcome: You take the wall down, in your head, and put the cab-yard in the middle, and all the strings lead to it. It is wonderfully neat. It fills the room with a clear, cold, satisfying sense of a case at last explained, and you feel it, with a distant uneasiness, as one feels the warm weather before a storm.

options.label: Take the Cards Down and Call It Four Cases.
options.detail: A widow, a clerk, a study and a cabman. Four accidents may be four accidents, and a detective who sees a hand behind every coincidence is someone who has read too many novels.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are pale, Holmes. Four things have happened in London in January, and each has a cause, and none of the causes need be the same. Go to bed.

options.outcome: You do not argue. You take the cards down, one at a time, and put them in a drawer, and the brown paper on the wall is blank. The lamp is out by midnight. It is the sensible, tired, honest thing to do. It will be a long time before you forgive yourself for it.

echoes.text: The nurse's testimonial at Lauder is signed J. Moriarty, M.A.
The guarantor's bond at Cowley and Vane is signed J. Moriarty.
A Professor J. Moriarty is on the subscribers' list in Fetter Lane.
A character reference for Gilbert Crane is signed J. Moriarty.

P10.title: The Same Hand
P10.description: Tuesday 1 February 1887, early. The name is on the table in front of you in a clean, firm schoolmaster's script, four times, on four kinds of paper, and a quarter of London has seen it. It is not in the Directory. It is not in Who's Who, or the Army List, or the Medical Register. It is the name of anyone who has, with a deliberate hand, put himself at the bottom of a number of pages that other people have forgotten to look at. You have the morning, and a table full of the ways in which a man may be looked for. Three of them are good, and the fourth is the Yard.

options.label: Write to the Provincial University Named on the Testimonial.
options.detail: Someone who signs M.A. and says that he was late of a chair has a college. A college has a register, and a register is a fact.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: To the Registrar. Sir, I should be obliged for the dates of the tenure of the late Professor J. Moriarty, and the reason of its ending. I enclose a stamped envelope, and a card. You will understand that I wish to be discreet.

options.outcome: It is a plain, civil letter, and you put it in the first post. It will be answered by return, or it will not be answered, and either way will tell you what you want. A person who has been removed from a chair in his twenties has a history, and a history is a thing that a college does not forget.

options.label: Ask Mycroft Whether the Name Is in Whitehall's Books.
options.detail: Your brother sees what the Government has not yet noticed. If the name has crossed a desk, he has seen it, and he will say so, with that dreadful, patient slowness.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: I do not know the name, Sherlock. I know the shape that it makes. There have been four small matters at the Foreign Office, each of which was disposed of cleanly, and none of which I could explain. I will have the papers sent to you.

options.outcome: It is as near to an alarm as you have ever seen him show. He has not the name, and he has the hole where the name should be. It is a curious thing to be told by your brother that he has been looking at the same absence for a year.

options.label: Go to the British Museum and Read What a Man Like That Writes.
options.detail: A professor of mathematics has put his work into print, and print is public. Anyone who is careful of his signature will be vain of his books.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: A treatise on the binomial theorem, published at twenty-one, and read by nobody. A work on the dynamics of an asteroid, published in the 'seventies, and understood by perhaps six living men. It is the work of a mind that is a great deal larger than its subject.

options.outcome: You spend a long day in the Reading Room, among the dust and the spectacles, and come out at closing time with a head full of mathematics and a deep distaste. You cannot follow the proofs. You can follow the man. He is exact, and cold, and a great deal cleverer than anybody has been willing to say.

echoes.text: The same hand has been in four places. It is not the hand of a person who thinks that he will be looked for.

P11.title: The Wrong Thread
P11.description: Tuesday 1 February 1887, the forenoon. Rudd's Yard in Southwark is a long, dank, cobbled place with a dozen cabs under a lean-to and a smell of horses and wet straw. The master is a broad, stolid, defensive man in a leather apron, who has been expecting you for a week and has decided to be offended. He has a ledger. He has a cabman who was seen last on the morning of the trial. He has a windfall that he says was a legacy. He looks at you with an air of virtuous obstinacy, and you realise, slowly, that you have no case against him at all.

options.label: Take Rudd to the Yard and Make Him Talk.
options.detail: Someone who has a windfall and a vanished cabman has a story. A night in the cells will make it plain, and Lestrade will be glad to have it.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: You've brought me a cab-yard owner with a legacy and a clean book, Mr Holmes. I'll put him in a cell, if you like. I'd as soon put the Archbishop of Canterbury in one.

options.outcome: He goes with you in sullen silence. By nightfall it is clear that he is exactly what he says. The legacy is real, and the cabman is a coincidence, and an unfortunate man has spent a night in a cell for a reason that nobody can explain to him. The papers say that Mr Sherlock Holmes has made a mistake.

options.label: Admit That the Thread Is Red and Start Again.
options.detail: A good detective is known by what he drops. It will cost you three days, and your pride, and the sense that you have been steered.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: I have lost three days on a cab-yard, and somebody has meant me to. It is a piece of tidy work. Somebody who knew that I should look for a thread has left me one, and a good one.

options.outcome: You walk out of the yard with your hands in your pockets and a distinct, slightly absurd sense of being watched from the roofs. It is a long, silent, tired walk to the river. You stand on the bridge for a while, and then you take a cab home, and begin the whole of it again.

options.label: Go Back to the Four Names and Look at Them Again.
options.detail: A person who has been led astray by a cab-yard has the names still. They are in the drawer, in the same ink, and there are enough of them to read.
options.outcome: You turn on your heel in the yard, to the amazement of Mr Rudd, and take a cab to Baker Street. The names are on the table, and you lay them side by side, and the whole of it comes out of the paper at once. You have lost a morning, and you have saved a winter.
options.requiresHint: Needs the name in three of the four cases

P12.title: The Examiner
P12.description:
Wednesday 2 February 1887, evening. What there is to be known about Professor James Moriarty has been got out of the registers, the Museum and a clerk's reluctant memory in two days, and it fits on a single sheet. He was a mathematical prodigy, who wrote a treatise at twenty-one and won a chair in a provincial university on the strength of it, and who left that chair within a few years, without a reference.

Since then he has coached young men for the Army, in a modest house in a modest suburb. He has no debts, no vices, no friends. He is, by every record, the most respectable man in London.

options.label: Go to the Provincial University and Find Out Why He Left.
options.detail: Anyone who is removed from a chair at twenty-five has done something. A college will keep the story in an old man's head, not in a register.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: It is the one thing in the whole career that is not in print. A mathematician of genius, and a chair, and a resignation in a single term. I shall go by the night mail, and I shall not tell my landlady where.

options.outcome: You take the night train to the North, in a second-class carriage, with a rug and a pipe. The ground lies white and flat under the moon, and you think about the sort of man who is the cleverest in a room and does not tell anybody. You sleep very little, and arrive at the grey, cold, dripping college at eight.

options.label: Read the Treatise and Look for the Man in It.
options.detail: A book that nobody can follow is a book that was written for one reader. If you can find where it hesitates, you will have found where he does.
options.outcome: It is a real discovery, and you do not know what it means. A dedication in a book of that kind, in a hand that cannot spare a word, is a piece of history. You ring for the tea, and make a note on the back of an envelope, and decide that you will go North after all.

options.label: Take a Cab to His Suburb and Look at the House.
options.detail: Someone who lives in a modest house in a modest street has a front door, and a front door has a number of small faces behind it. You need only to see them go in and out.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: A neat brick house, with a monkey-puzzle tree and a brass plate that says nothing. A tall, stooping, grey figure at an upper window, who looked down at the road for a second and turned away. He did not look at me. He looked at the cab.

options.outcome: You sit in the hansom for an hour, with the blind half down. A great many respectable men go in and out of the gate, with parcels and satchels and a single, surprising look of anxiety. It is not a school, and it is not a club.

echoes.text: You have lost three days on a cab-yard. It is the thing that you will not say to Watson.
Mycroft has told you of four small matters at the Foreign Office, which were disposed of cleanly.

P13.title: The Provincial University
P13.description: Thursday 3 February 1887, morning. The college has a tower, a quad, a porter's lodge and a fine drizzle, and every one of them is grey. The Registrar's letter has not come. The Dean is at a meeting. An old porter in a green apron has been standing at the lodge door for forty years. He has a long memory and a short temper, and he has been told that you are a gentleman from the Ecclesiastical Commissioners. He looks at your boots. He says that he remembers Professor Moriarty. He says it as one speaks of someone who has been dead a long time, and who is not.

options.label: Ask the Old Porter What Became of the Student.
options.detail: A porter keeps a college's secrets in his pockets. If a man left in disgrace, there was a person on the other side of it, and the porter will know the name and the year.

quote.speaker: The old porter
quote.text: There was a lad, sir, a nice quiet lad, in his second year. The Professor was fond of him. He was found drowned in the canal in the March of 'seventy-nine, and the Professor never lectured again. They said it was a dark rumour, and I'll say no more.

options.outcome: He says it in a low, dry, careful voice, and pulls his apron straight. It is the story that is not in print. A student, a death, a resignation and a rumour that is better forgotten. You thank him, and he does not look at the half-sovereign, and takes it. That is the first time that you have felt anything like pity for the man whom you have been hunting.

options.label: Ask the Dean for the College's Own Account.
options.detail: A Dean will give you the official version, which is the version that he has rehearsed. It will be dry, and decent, and it will tell you what the college has been willing to say.

quote.speaker: The Dean
quote.text: Professor Moriarty resigned for reasons of health, Mr Holmes, and the college has the greatest regard for his work. I am not at liberty to say more. I will say that it was an exceptionally sad business, and that we were all sorry for it.

options.outcome: He gives you sherry, and shakes your hand, and sees you to the gate. It is the entirely courteous, wholly useless account of an institution that has agreed to forget. You take it down in your notebook word for word, because you have learned that the words that a college chooses are the shape of what it is concealing.

options.label: Go Away and Say That You Have Not Been.
options.detail: A person who comes and goes without leaving a name has spoken to nobody. It is a clean, cowardly, prudent course, and it spares you the rumour.
options.outcome: You catch the afternoon train, with a rug on your knees and a feeling that you have wasted two days. It is a long way back to London. You look out at the grey country as it goes past, and decide that anyone who is the most respectable man in London has taken a great deal of trouble to be so.

P14.title: The Nurse of Lauder
P14.description: Friday 4 February 1887, afternoon. She is not in Edinburgh, and not in Lauder. She is in a tall, shabby tenement in Leith, in two rooms at the top, with the blinds down and a bolt on the door. It has taken Lestrade's men and an Edinburgh agent three weeks to find her, and she has been told that you are coming. She is a plain, tired, middle-aged woman in a black dress, who has been a nurse for twenty years, and she looks at you, when she lets you in, as at the bailiff. There is a trunk in the corner that is already packed.

options.label: Persuade Her to Say What She Saw at Lauder.
options.detail: A nurse who has been paid to be elsewhere knows what happened in the room. It is a matter of making her feel that she has a witness, and that she has a friend.

quote.speaker: Mrs Dunbar
quote.text: I did nothing, sir. I gave her the medicine, as the doctor ordered. But there was a visit, in the night, and a gentleman who was not the doctor. He did not stay a quarter of an hour. And afterwards I was told to take a holiday.

success.outcome: She is silent for a minute, and then she begins to speak, in a dry, quick, low voice, as if it were a thing that she had said many times to the wall. A tall gentleman in a tall hat, who gave her thirty pounds and a testimonial. A colonel with a huge moustache who sat by the bed for ten minutes in the dark. And in the morning, a woman who had died in her sleep.

failure.outcome: She says that she has told the Yard everything, and that she is going to Canada, and that you may take your questions to the devil. She does not weep, and she does not argue, and when you stand up the bolt is shot behind you. By the time that Lestrade's man has the door open she is gone, and the trunk with her.

options.label: Offer Her a Passage and a Little Money to Say Nothing to Anyone Else.
options.detail: A frightened witness who is paid to go away is a witness who is safe. It is an ugly way of keeping a person, and it will keep her alive.

quote.speaker: Mrs Dunbar
quote.text: I'll tell you all of it, sir, if you'll take me out of the country. I've been three weeks in this room with a trunk, waiting for a knock, and I've never had such a thing in my life. Is it true that you're paid by nobody?

options.outcome: You say that it is wholly true. She tells it in an hour, with her hands folded, and when she has done, you arrange for a berth on a Liverpool boat. She will be in New York by the end of the month. It is a bad, sad, practical bargain, and you are not in the least proud of it, and you are fairly sure that it is the right one.

options.label: Leave Her to Her Trunk and Her Bolt.
options.detail: A woman who is frightened and in hiding is safe where she is, and a visit may bring somebody after you. It is an unkind prudence, and a considered one.

quote.speaker: Your own notebook
quote.text: She will be gone by Monday, and I shall have nothing from her, and somebody will have found her in a week. I have not been to see her, and I have been. It is the oddest sort of non-visit that I have ever paid.

options.outcome: You stand at the bottom of the tenement stair, in the grey Leith light, and look up at the blinds. A small hand puts one of them aside, and drops it. You walk away down the street without turning your head.

P15.title: The Colonel at Cards
P15.description: Monday 7 February 1887, nine in the evening. Colonel Sebastian Moran, late of the Indian Army, has the end table at the Bagatelle Card Club, where he has had it for three winters. He is a lean, brown, grizzled man with a bald forehead and a huge moustache, and he plays whist with the placid, patient, absent air of a tiger on a branch. You have been shown to the gallery by a steward who has a good memory for faces, and none at all for what they are doing. Nothing on earth is more ordinary than a retired officer playing cards. You have a note in your pocket that says that he has been paid every month for four years by a firm of agents in Lincoln's Inn.

options.label: Watch the Colonel and the Man Who Joins Him After Midnight.
options.detail: Someone who is paid by an agent meets a person who is paid by a principal. There is somebody who will come to the table at one, and somebody who will leave with him.
options.outcome: You do not see his face. You see the hat, and the shoulders, and the odd slow movement of the head from side to side, like a snake that has been told to wait. It is the same hat that was in a country lane in Berwickshire, and in a street in Southwark, and it is on the head of someone who has just given an order to the best shot in India.

options.label: Ask the Steward Who Pays the Colonel's Subscriptions.
options.detail: A club has a subscription book, and a subscription is paid by a cheque or by a person. The Colonel does not look like anyone who pays his own.

quote.speaker: The steward
quote.text: It's paid by his agents, sir, Messrs Rolfe and Dale, of Lincoln's Inn. Always by the first of the month, and always in a cheque with an unusual signature. I've often noticed it. It's a firm sort of hand.

options.outcome: He gives you the name of the firm and the date of the last cheque. It is as dull as a sum, and it is the second place where the same copperplate has appeared. You make a note of the signature, and the steward's eyebrows, and he says that it is always a pleasure to assist a gentleman who takes an interest.

options.label: Go Down and Sit at the Colonel's Table.
options.detail: A person who sits down opposite a tiger is not safe, and is within reach. It is the one way to see his hands, and to know whether he cheats.

quote.speaker: Colonel Moran
quote.text: You are a stranger, sir, and a pale one. I should not play with me if I were you. I have been told that I am unlucky for those who do not know me, and I have never found it otherwise.

options.outcome: He says it with a thin smile, and deals. You lose four pounds, with great care, and rise from the table at the end of the rubber. He watches you go. This is the first time in your life that you have looked at a person who has killed for hire and known, without a doubt, that you were looking at one.

echoes.text: The nurse spoke of a colonel with a huge moustache. You did not need her to name him.

P16.title: Mycroft's Warning
P16.description:
Tuesday 8 February 1887, ten at night. The Strangers' Room of the Diogenes Club is cold, and the fire has not been lit. Mycroft is sitting upright in his chair with a file on his knee that he has not opened. He has been told by a friend of a friend that you have been seen at the Bagatelle, and in Leith, and in front of a house in Kensington.

He has been told it by three people, in three days, in three different forms. He looks at you with a long, grave, familiar sorrow, as at a boy who has found a snake in the garden.

options.label: Ask Him to Open the File.
options.detail: Anyone who has a file of four small matters at the Foreign Office has more than a hunch. He has a pattern, and a pattern is a thing that he does not lend.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: There have been four matters, Sherlock. A despatch copied, a cipher changed, a clerk who left, a minister who was told something that he should not have been. Each was done by a different hand. I do not believe that they were different.

options.outcome: He opens it, and you read it on your knee. It is a dry, short, anxious little file, in his small hand. There is nothing in it that would convince a jury, and it has exactly the shape of your own wall. He says, stiffly, that he is relieved that somebody else can see it.

options.label: Ask Him to Keep Out of It and Let You Work Alone.
options.detail: Someone who is known to be Mycroft's brother is someone who is watched. If the Professor sees that the Government is looking, he will go quiet, and a quiet professor is no use to anyone.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
